caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
scenario: A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

options.A: Recommend avoiding heavy lifting, initiate β-blocker therapy, and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week
options.B: Obtain blood cultures, begin empiric antibiotics, and admit with telemetry
options.C: Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements, perform a triple rule-out chest computed tomographic angiogram, and admit to observation
options.D: Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department

answer: Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department
distractors: Recommend avoiding heavy lifting, initiate β-blocker therapy, and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week
Obtain blood cultures, begin empiric antibiotics, and admit with telemetry
Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements, perform a triple rule-out chest computed tomographic angiogram, and admit to observation
explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

caption: A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.
scenario: A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
explanation: C. Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

scenario: A man in his early 50s presented with recurrent episodes of cough, palpitations, shortness of breath, and exertional chest pain. He had a history of type 2 diabetes but had no history of smoking or other cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. There was no family history of sudden cardiac death. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an ST-segment elevation in leads V1and V2(Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a right lung mass, and coronary CT angiography indicated stenosis in the right coronary and left anterior descending coronary arteries.

options.D: Perform genetic testing to confirm an SCN5A variant

distractors: Conduct a sodium channel blocker drug provocation test
Perform genetic testing to confirm an SCN5A variant
explanation: Acute myocardial ischemia with Brugada phenocopy A. Perform emergency coronary angiography Emergency coronary angiography confirmed near-complete occlusion of the right coronary artery, which was successfully treated with stent implantation. There was diffuse stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending branch, measuring 60% at its most severe point. Following the procedure, the ECG results normalized and the Brugada-like pattern resolved (Figure 2). Brugada syndrome1is a genetic disorder associated with variants in theSCN5Agene,2leading to abnormal ion channel function and increased risk of sudden cardiac death. In contrast, Brugada phenocopies can be induced by reversible conditions, such as myocardial ischemia,3,4pulmonary embolism, electrolyte imbalances, or drug effects.5In this case, the patient had no electrolyte imbalance or pulmonary embolism. The Brugada type 1 pattern on the initial ECG was likely caused by transient ischemia in the right ventricular outflow tract due to severe coronary artery stenosis. The resolution of the ECG abnormalities following revascularization supports the diagnosis of a Brugada phenocopy rather than true Brugada syndrome. This case underscores the importance of distinguishing between true Brugada syndrome and Brugada phenocopy, particularly in patients with reversible underlying causes, such as myocardial ischemia. Accurate diagnosis is essential for guiding appropriate treatment and improving patient outcomes. Clinicians should be aware of the potential for Brugada-like ECG patterns in the context of acute coronary syndromes and other reversible conditions. The patient was subsequently discharged to continue outpatient treatment at the local hospital. He was treated conservatively for the lung tumor at the local hospital, during which no further Brugada-like ECG patterns were observed.

caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram with apical 4-chamber views showing severe mitral regurgitation at a heart rate of 95 beats per minute (bpm), with wide QRS on monitoring (A), and minimal mitral regurgitation at a resting heart rate of 58 bpm, with narrow QRS on monitoring (B).
scenario: A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

options.B: Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
options.D: β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

answer: Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
distractors: β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB
explanation: Rate-related LBBB resulting in acute severe MR B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

caption: Findings on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) prior to initiating interleukin-1 (IL-1) receptor therapy in this patient. Initial cardiac MRI phase-sensitive inversion recovery sequences in the sagittal section depicting pericardial thickening and circumferential pericardial effusion (prior to any therapy) (A) and moderate late gadolinium enhancement (after nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and colchicine therapy, prior to IL-1 receptor antagonist therapy) (B). Arrowheads depict the pericardium.
scenario: A woman aged in her late 20s presented for follow-up regarding her chest pain. Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

options.A: Continue current therapy with tapering after improvement in markers and cardiac MRI
options.B: Initiate IL-1ras for shorter than recommended duration with current therapy wean
options.C: Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean

answer: Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean
distractors: Continue current therapy with tapering after improvement in markers and cardiac MRI
Initiate IL-1ras for shorter than recommended duration with current therapy wean
explanation: C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean The advent of steroid-sparing IL-1ras like anakinra and rilonacept has revolutionized chronic recurrent pericarditis (ChRP) treatment. While IL-1ras offer targeted IL-1α/IL-1β pathway inhibition, concerns about long-term malignancy risk affect treatment decisions, especially in those with recent or familial cancer history. The AIRTRIP1and RHAPSODY2clinical trials excluded patients with cancer within the last 5 years, making extrapolation challenging and creating provider and patient uncertainty regarding IL-1ra use in this context. These concerns stem from IL-1’s dual role in cancer biology. While primarily recognized for its protumoral effects, IL-1 may paradoxically inhibit cancer development in certain contexts.3Combined IL-1α/IL-1β inhibition may amplify this effect, yet clinical evidence validating these cellular concerns is lacking.4Fleischmann and colleagues’ review of anakinra in rheumatoid arthritis5suggests a decreased long-term malignancy risk, attributed to reduced systemic inflammation. Although lymphoma and melanoma incidence increased in this cohort, causality with anakinra remained inconclusive. While no firm guidelines endorse regular screening for these specific cancers in patients receiving IL-1ra therapy, consideration should be given to those with significant risk factors. Bilal and colleagues6reviewed cancer risk associated with long-term IL inhibitor use, suggesting an increased risk correlating with treatment duration. Analysis of studies including rilonacept use by Schumacher and colleagues reported isolated cases of prostate cancer and leg squamous cell carcinoma during phase II and III trials.7,8In the RHAPSODY trial,21 case of squamous cell carcinoma was reported. Notably, therapy discontinuation was not necessary for any event. Considering this evidence, malignancy risk does not appear to be significant with long-term IL-1ra use. Generalizability limitations include follow-up duration, as prolonged IL-1 inhibition might trigger cancer in genetically predisposed individuals. While malignancy diagnosis may be limited by follow-up, no malignancies were reported during the open-label study spanning 72 to 96 weeks of rilonacept treatment for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.9Whether IL-1ras unmask or cause cancer in such cases or are innocent bystanders would be challenging to address. For patients with prior malignancies, a shared decision-making process with an oncologist is advised. This allows weighing the risks of untreated ChRP against cancer recurrence. Limited data hinder estimating recurrence risk with IL-1ra therapy, particularly in patients with frequent flares. Nevertheless, in certain cases, oncological consultation is invaluable for assessing recurrence risk and increasing confidence in IL-1ra use for suitable patients. However, these recommendations become more diluted in those with a family history of cancer, even with suspected genetic syndromes, as in this patient. If the guidelines for screening of the specific cancers are followed, a reasonable counsel can be provided to the patients in need regarding IL-1ra therapy for treating recurrent pericarditis. Extension of therapy beyond recommended durations, like 18 to 24 months for rilonacept, can be considered on a case-by-case basis depending on the interim development of suspicious lesions found on screening vs the current pericarditis status. Additionally, using prophylactic measures in select cases to prevent the development of malignancies in genetically predisposed individuals may increase confidence in prescribing IL-1ras.10 Further genetic testing did not identify a sequence variation. After a shared decision, rilonacept was started, allowing the patient to taper off ibuprofen and colchicine within 10 weeks with no further symptoms. While taking rilonacept, she increased physical activity and showed reduced pericardial enhancement on cardiac MRI. She has been closely monitored for premalignant conditions, particularly breast and cervical cancer, and has been free of such conditions after 1 year of therapy.

caption: Admission electrocardiogram (ECG) showing type A preexcitation syndrome, with an upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and positive T waves in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave. These changes were suggestive of a de Winter ECG pattern.
scenario: A man in his mid-50s presented to the emergency department with chest pain that had persisted for 30 minutes without relief. Two years prior to presentation, he had been admitted for treatment of non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (non-STEMI). Twenty years ago, he had a history of tachycardia because of preexcitation syndrome that was terminated with medication. On presentation to the emergency department, the patient’s temperature was 36.5 °C; heart rate, 75 beats/min; and blood pressure, 100/60 mm Hg. His initial electrocardiogram (ECG) is shown inFigure 1. The initial troponin I level was normal.

options.A: Cardiac echocardiography and repeat troponin I measurement
options.B: Coronary enhanced CT and repeat troponin I measurement
options.C: Monitor and treat for non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome
options.D: Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI

answer: Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI
distractors: Cardiac echocardiography and repeat troponin I measurement
Coronary enhanced CT and repeat troponin I measurement
Monitor and treat for non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome
explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

caption: Initial electrocardiogram demonstrating sinus tachycardia with ST-segment elevations of 1.0 mm in lead I; 2.0 mm in leads II, III, and the augmented vector foot (aVF); and 2.0 to 5.0 mm in the precordial leads. Widened QRS complexes and low-voltage complexes in the limb leads were observed. aVR indicates augmented vector right.
scenario: A woman in her mid-20s with no relevant medical history presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of fever, chest pain, and exertional dyspnea. An initial electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus tachycardia, QRS widening (130 milliseconds), low-voltage complexes in the limb leads, and tombstonelike convex ST-segment elevation (STE) in most leads, particularly V1 through V6 (Figure 1). Transient second-degree atrioventricular block was observed on ambulatory ECG monitoring. Her blood pressure was 81/50 mm Hg. The N-terminal pro–brain-type natriuretic peptide was 10 099 pg/mL (to convert to ng/L, multiply by 1; reference value, <150) and the troponin I level was 22 ng/mL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1; reference value, <0.016). No obstructive stenosis was seen on coronary computed tomography angiography. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed symmetric left ventricular (LV) wall thickening (septal thickness, 16 mm) and reduced LV systolic function with an ejection fraction of 35%.
explanation: The diagnosis of fulminant myocarditis (FM) was confirmed subsequently by endomyocardial biopsy, which demonstrated extensive and diffuse lymphocytic infiltration, severe interstitial edema, and slightly myocyte necrosis (Figure 2A). Due to cardiogenic shock, an intra-aortic balloon pump was implemented soon after admission, combined with glucocorticoids and intravenous immunoglobulins. On the sixth day after admission, the intra-aortic balloon pump was removed, and a repeat ECG showed that the STE had decreased nearly to baseline, with diffuse T-wave inversion and Q waves in V1 to V3 (Figure 2B). Concomitantly, repeat ECG revealed that both LV wall thickness and LV ejection fraction were restored to the normal range. Subsequent cardiac magnetic imaging showed no late-gadolinium enhancement. FM represents the most acute and life-threatening manifestation of myocarditis, characterized by sudden onset and rapid clinical deterioration, with left and/or right ventricular dysfunction, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and the need for pharmacological and/or mechanical circulatory support.1In this patient, tombstonelike STE in extensive leads was indicative of severe myocardial injury. This is more commonly seen in ST-elevation myocardial infarction, but a diagnostic hallmark in FM is that there is no ST-segment depression in the reciprocal leads as would be seen in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Additionally, ST segments are elevated in lead augmented vector right in FM, while they are usually depressed in acute pericarditis.2Lead augmented vector right has also been characterized in pericarditis or myocarditis by elevation of the PR interval. However, this change is often subtle in FM.2 The increased LV wall thickness in FM is due to the intense inflammatory response seen on endomyocardial biopsy. Interstitial edema contributes not only to the wall thickening, but also to the decreased ventricular contractility in this disorder.3Therefore, the low-voltage complexes, QRS widening, and transient second-degree atrioventricular block in this patient were considered related to myocardial edema and inflammation, in line with the myocardial pathology. A QRS interval greater than 120 milliseconds on ECG emerged as an adverse prognostic factor associated with the long-term outcome of patients with FM.4The patient was confirmed on endomyocardial biopsy to have lymphocytic myocarditis, which ruled out giant cell myocarditis and eosinophilic myocarditis and helped to guide an appropriately immunosuppressive treatment regimen. After effective immunotherapy, the myocardial thickness recovered, the relevant ECG indicators improved, and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging also suggested resolution of the myocardial edema. At 5-year follow-up after discharge, the patient felt well, and echocardiography revealed normal LV size, wall thickness, and ejection fraction. The ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with left anterior fascicular blocks; flat T waves in leads II, III, and augmented vector foot, and poor R-wave progression in leads V1 to V3 (Figure 2B).

scenario: A woman in her mid-60s with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) and hypertension presented to an outlying hospital with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had been diagnosed with AF 3 months prior and was prescribed flecainide, 100 mg twice daily; metoprolol; and apixaban. She was also taking furosemide, 40 mg twice daily. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, mild mitral regurgitation, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. An electrocardiogram (ECG) obtained 1 month before presentation showed sinus rhythm, PR interval of 190 milliseconds, and QRS interval of 100 milliseconds. On presentation, she was anxious appearing, mildly dyspneic, and tachycardic, with a heart rate of 130 bpm. Blood pressure was 94/52 mm Hg. Her mentation was normal, and she denied chest pain. Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed a monomorphic, wide complex tachycardia at 130 bpm with a QRS duration of 220 milliseconds and right bundle branch morphology. Laboratory testing was notable for acute kidney injury, with a creatinine level of 4.0 mg/dL (baseline, 1.4 mg/dL; to convert to micromoles per liter, multiply by 88.4) (estimated glomerular filtration rate, 12 mL/min/1.73 m2); troponin I, 0.029 ng/mL (reference range, <0.04 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1); sodium, 132 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); potassium, 5.1 mEq/L (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 1); and normal values of serum magnesium, calcium, and phosphorus.
explanation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block, and severe intraventricular conduction delay due to flecainide toxicity D. Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction. Flecainide slows atrial conduction, thereby slowing the rate of AFL (typically approximately 300 bpm) as seen in this patient (to approximately 260 bpm), and, if not given concomitantly with a β-blocker, may result in 1:1 AV nodal conduction resulting in ventricular fibrillation. The differential diagnosis of a wide complex tachycardia with flecainide use includes supraventricular tachycardia (including AFL) with 1:1 or 2:1 block and aberrancy, intraventricular conduction delay (IVCD), preexcitation, and VT.8 Mortality due to flecainide toxicity may be as high as 22%. The mainstay of treatment is sodium bicarbonate administration to reverse the sodium channel blockade through competitive inhibition and to alkalize the serum pH, which facilitates flecainide dissociation from its sodium channel binding sites; the pH goal should be 7.55, and the serum sodium level should be 150 mEq/L.4,9The dose is a 1-mEq/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 15 to 20 mEq/h. In refractory cases, intravenous lipid emulsion therapy may be tried—this serves as a “lipid sink” to remove lipophilic drugs, such as flecainide, from the circulation. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation may be needed in profound shock. The patient was treated with sodium bicarbonate. The QRS interval progressively narrowed with the rhythm first changing to AF and then spontaneously reverting to sinus rhythm, PR interval of 195 milliseconds, nonspecific IVCD (QRS interval of 112 milliseconds), and prolonged QTc interval (504 milliseconds). A serum flecainide measurement ordered on admission was available on day 2 and was 1.42 μg/mL (reference range, 0.2-0.9 μg/mL); the serum creatinine level improved to 1.6 mg/dL after intravenous fluids were administered. She was discharged on hospital day 3 and was doing well at 1-month follow-up. If AF recurs, she has opted for catheter ablation.

scenario: A patient in his mid-60s with a history of interstitial pulmonary fibrosis underwent bilateral orthotopic lung transplant (BOLT) 6 months earlier. He was hospitalized for sepsis from pneumonia complicated by acute transplant rejection, without any cardiac symptoms. Coronary angiography prior to BOLT showed no evidence of coronary artery disease. His only cardiac history was tricuspid valve repair at the time of BOLT. His baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) is shown inFigure 1A. He progressed to having severe acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring intubation. As he continued to worsen, the decision was made to paralyze him a few hours later. Changes on telemetry were noted. Shortly thereafter, 12-lead ECG showed the changes inFigure 1B.

explanation: Apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles D. Redo the ECG with new leads and new lead positioning This patient’s broad T-wave inversions occurred shortly after paralysis and were artifactual. His troponin level was normal, and echocardiography revealed normal wall motion. His metabolic panel showed no electrolyte derangements. The ECG inFigure 1B is not typical for pericarditis. The abnormal ECG findings were due to apical pulsation caused by paralysis of the intercostal muscles underlying the precordial leads. With application of external pressure to the precordial leads along the intercostal space, ST-segment changes resolved (Figure 2A). Of note, true ST depressions were noted after manual compression (Figure 2A). These ST depressions were thought to be due to profound hypoxia and subendocardial ischemia. The arterial waveform can be seen transmitting through the terminal portion of the QRS complex, creating superimposition or merging of the ECG and arterial line waveforms (Figure 2B). While leads V1and V2were normal, V3through V6displayed tall T-waves and abnormalities of the ST segment that were not transmitted through any of the other precordial leads, likely due to placement of leads V3through V6over the intercostal muscles. The limb leads were also affected in this case because leads II and III were placed on the upper abdomen to avoid entanglement with other lines and tubes. Paralysis of the intercostal muscles likely resulted in direct transmission of the apical impulse to the ECG leads. Review of telemetry showed this ECG change occurring immediately after the patient was intubated and paralyzed. Physical palpation revealed a subtle, left parasternal lift most prominent over lead V4. Pulse-congruent ECG artifacts have been observed with prominent right radial arterial pulsation1and left forearm arteriovenous fistula,2and with left leg arterial pulsations.3These arterial pulse tapping artifacts are also known as the Aslanger sign.4There are no documented cases of artifact caused by apical impulse. The point of maximal impulse (PMI) refers to the location on the chest wall where contractions in systole are best palpated or visually observed, which correlates with the anatomic position of the cardiac apex. In healthy individuals, the PMI typically occurs as a single, unsustained tap for each systolic contraction palpable over a 2- to 3-cm area at the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. With loss of intercostal muscle tension, the cardiac impulse may be more easily transmitted to the apical leads. The patient was eventually placed on venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation due to worsening hypoxic respiratory failure in the setting of multifocal pneumonia and transplant rejection. He was treated with a course of steroids and broad-spectrum antibiotics. He was then decannulated and underwent tracheostomy. He was eventually discharged after a prolonged hospital course.

scenario: A man in his 50s underwent clinical assessment for a 4-month history of recurrent palpitations, fatigue, and progressive exertion dyspnea. He had no history of cardiac disease, and there was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. Physical examination revealed an irregular pulse and a systolic murmur at the heart apex. Holter monitoring and 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings documented irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia in an incessant, repetitive fashion with heart rates up to 180 beats per minute and occasional short runs of wide-QRS tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated and diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 30%) associated with moderate to severe functional mitral regurgitation. Blood test results were within normal limits, including thyroid function, C-reactive protein, and myocardial enzymes. The patient was hospitalized, and medical therapy was initiated, including ACE inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, β-blockers, and diuretics. Coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary stenoses. A representative 12-lead ECG of the arrhythmia is shown inFigure 1.

distractors: Optimize medical therapy for 3 months, and implant a defibrillator if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement is obtained
Perform transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair
explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

scenario: A woman in her 90s presented to the emergency department with symptoms of fever, hemoptysis, and syncopal episodes. She had a history of breast cancer and pulmonary nodules with biopsy findings negative for metastatic disease but positive for granulomatous inflammation. Initial vital signs included blood pressure of 103/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 190 bpm, and temperature of 38.7 °C. Electrocardiogram showed monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a morphology suggesting right ventricular (RV) origin (Figure 1). In addition to receiving intravenous amiodarone hydrochloride, she had correction of mild hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L [reference range, 3.5-5.2 mEq/L]; to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 1.0). Successful arrhythmia termination occurred shortly thereafter, and her vital signs remained stable. Chest computed tomographic angiography excluded pulmonary embolism but showed pulmonary nodules and mediastinal lymphadenopathy that had progressed compared with her previous computed tomography. An echocardiogram showed severe RV and left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction with multiple areas of hypokinesis.
explanation: A. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging The patient underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, which demonstrated areas of nonischemic near-transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) of the interventricular septum and epicardium to midmyocardium of the LV basal to midanterior and basal inferior walls extending to the RV walls and septal papillary muscle (Figure 2A). However, T2 mapping revealed only discrete evidence of edema of a small region of the midanterior LV wall. Taken together, these findings raised the possibility of end-stage cardiac sarcoidosis (CS). Cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose F 18 (FDG) and rubidium-82 positron emission tomography (PET) for CS was obtained with a strict high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet, followed by 12 hours of fasting prior to the examination per American Society of Nuclear Cardiology recommendations.1Because the patient was hospitalized, dietary compliance was ensured. Furthermore, FDG uptake was segmental and the LV blood pool maximum standard uptake value was only 1.1, demonstrating adequate suppression of normal myocardial glucose utilization. There was an extensive FDG uptake (Figure 2B), with maximum standard uptake value of 10.4 in the LV septum. There was also extracardiac FDG uptake in hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and in multiple pulmonary nodules. Rubidium-82 PET showed only mildly reduced perfusion in the basal to apical septal wall. This case highlights multiple learning points in the use of multimodality imaging for evaluation of patients with CS and understanding its complex pathophysiology. First, the utility of T2 mapping for detecting myocardial edema, a potential surrogate for active inflammation, needs to be better understood, as this can be challenging and in this case underrepresented the extensive positive FDG uptake seen on cardiac PET. Despite extensive LV and RV LGE and depressed biventricular systolic function, substantial myocardial inflammation in this patient is consistent with active rather than end-stage CS. Second, determining individual patient prognosis and assessment of immunosuppression response in patients with CS using cardiac imaging remains challenging. It has been demonstrated that patients without LGE are at an extremely low risk of arrhythmic events.2,3However, although there is increased risk of arrhythmic events in patients with cardiac involvement identified by LGE, only a fraction of these patients experience arrhythmic events. Patients with both RV and LV LGE are at elevated risk of cardiovascular events compared with patients with only LV enhancement.2-4Last, while CS is extremely rare after 70 years of age, as the oldest patient reported in the literature was 80 years old,5this patient presented with CS in her 90s, reminding us that CS remains on the differential diagnosis in patients with sustained ventricular arrythmias regardless of age. Heart failure guideline–directed medical treatment, oral amiodarone, and immunosuppressive therapy consisting of a high, tapering dose of prednisone with mycophenolate mofetil were started. The patient remained stable with no more arrythmias. After shared decision discussions with the patient, a cardiac defibrillator was not implanted given the patient’s age and out of respect for her wishes. She will undergo follow-up FDG-PET to monitor her response to therapy and disease activity.

scenario: A woman in her early 40s, gravida 3, para 3, with a history of migraines and recurrent preeclampsia and who was 11 weeks post partum presented with acute pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath, and nausea that started several hours after a flight from Florida to New York City. She was noted to have tachycardia (110 beats/min) and hypoxemia (90% receiving room air) with a blood pressure of 106/81 mm Hg. Cardiac, respiratory, and pulse examination results were unremarkable. She denied any clear physical or emotional triggers preceding presentation. Before presentation, the patient reported good health with satisfactory employment-mandated routine physical examinations. She denied a history of smoking, alcohol, or illicit drug use. She was not taking hormonal birth control or hormone therapy. Laboratory values demonstrated a normal complete blood cell count and metabolic panel. Chest radiograph results were unremarkable. A computed tomographic chest scan excluded pulmonary embolism but suggested pulmonary and interstitial edema. Results of an electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with premature ventricular contractions, subcentimeter ST-segment elevation in leads I and aVL and 1-mm ST-segment depression in leads II, III, aVF, and V5through V6. Initial high-sensitivity troponin was 110 000 ng/mL (to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). Results of cardiac point-of-care ultrasonography demonstrated a severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 40%, with hypokinesis of the anterolateral and posterior walls. Emergent cardiac catheterization revealed spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) of the left main coronary artery (Figure 1andVideo).
explanation: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection of the left main coronary artery SCAD has been increasingly recognized as an important cause of acute coronary syndromes, especially in young healthy women without traditional cardiovascular risk factors. The prevalence of SCAD is approximately 0.5% of patients who present with acute coronary syndromes.1Extracoronary fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), depression, rheumatoid arthritis, anxiety, genetic disorders, peripartum, and migraine disorder are associated with SCAD.2,3Genetic disorders, peripartum SCAD, and FMD were independent predictors of 3-year adverse cardiac events.4Although mortality is low, one-fourth of patients with SCAD had recurrent SCAD. There are important educational points from this case. First, in experienced, high-volume centers, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is safe in selected patients with SCAD with high-risk features. Conservative therapy may not be appropriate in patients with SCAD with high-risk features including ongoing ischemia, left main artery dissection, or hemodynamic instability.5In the 2 largest SCAD registries, PCI was appropriate and safe for patients with SCAD with high-risk features such as cardiogenic shock, active/ongoing ischemia, hemodynamic instability, ventricular arrhythmias, ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, and high-risk anatomy.4,5The role of intracoronary imaging is crucial to ensure that the wire is in the true lumen distally and to ensure that the stent covers the entire intramural hematoma. Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) should also be considered when PCI is technically challenging or has been attempted and unsuccessful.6,7Given the clinical scenario and angiographical features in this case, the decision was made to pursue revascularization, and PCI with a drug-eluting stent was successfully performed. Second, we demonstrated that radial approach is safe for patients with SCAD. In a meta-analysis of undergoing PCI, radial access was associated with a significant risk reduction in bleeding, vascular complications, and mortality compared with femoral access.8There are no data comparing radial vs femoral access in the subgroup of patients with SCAD undergoing PCI, particularly peripartum SCAD. Theoretically, femoral access could potentially cause more complications and bleeding due to its association with kidney FMD and arteriopathies compared with radial access. Third, pregnancy should be considered a high-risk feature in patients with SCAD. It has been hypothesized that hormonal changes and hemodynamic variations might be significant contributors to SCAD in pregnant patients by alterations in the architecture of the arterial wall, but the cause is unknown. Investigators suggested that unsuccessful PCI was common for SCAD in pregnant individuals (35%).5Three patients subsequently underwent CABG due to unsuccessful PCI, and 1 had CABG because of SCAD progression despite conservative management.5 Once SCAD is diagnosed, screening for FMD is needed.4Post PCI, lifelong low-dose aspirin is recommended. Other antiplatelet agents and duration of dual antiplatelet therapy after PCI is primarily tailored individually based on the location of SCAD, the number and size of stents used, etc. β-Blockers and cardiac rehabilitation are recommended in patients with SCAD; statins and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin-receptor blockers may be considered selectively when other clinical indications exist. Management of SCAD in pregnant patients can be challenging, particularly when the dissection involves the left main coronary artery. PCI performed at an experienced center can offer a good outcome for selected patients. Further study is needed to identify whether recurrent preeclampsia is a risk factor for SCAD in pregnant patients. The patient underwent PCI of the left main successfully without complications (Figure 2). The patient recovered well after PCI and returned safely to her hometown to undergo further evaluation for FMD and connective tissue disorders.

scenario: A woman in her late 60s presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. She described several other episodes occurring at rest over the past several weeks. She denied palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She was otherwise in excellent health and not taking any medications. She had no family history of syncope or sudden death. Her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) results were normal, but premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) were noted on telemetry. Shortly thereafter, 2 episodes of fast polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), 30 minutes apart, were recorded, both lasting less than 4 seconds (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG showed PVCs (Figure 1B). Laboratory test results including serum potassium and magnesium as well as 3 serial troponin levels were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function without wall motion abnormalities or valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed a 50% stenosis of the left circumflex artery. Instant wave-free ratio across the stenosis was 1.0.

options.B: Perform provocative drug testing with procainamide

distractors: Perform provocative drug testing with procainamide
explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

scenario: A man in his late 50s was released from a tertiary hospital with an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction and cardiogenic shock with onset 6 days before admission. On admission, vital signs showed blood pressure as 98/66 mm Hg while receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine from the referral hospital, a regular heart rate of 90 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute, peripheral oxygen saturation 96% nasal oxygen at 3 L per minute, and a temperature of 36.7° C. Echocardiography showed reduced left ventricle systolic function (estimated ejection fraction, 34%) and hypokinesia of the anteroseptal, anterior, anterolateral, and septal walls. Lung ultrasound demonstrated multiple B-lines in both lung fields. Diagnostic coronary angiography revealed a total occlusion in the left main coronary artery. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was successful in opening the osteal left main and drug-eluting stents were placed in the left main and left anterior descending arteries. Following PCI, the patient had episodes of supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Electrical cardioversion was performed and a loading dose of amiodarone was administered. Chest radiography during the loading dose of amiodarone showed infiltrates in both lung fields (Figure 1A). While in the intensive cardiovascular care unit, maintenance doses of amiodarone were continued because of episodes of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, and torsaded de pointes. On the third day of hospitalization, despite adequate diuresis, the chest radiography showed persistent pulmonary edema. Chest computed tomography showed a reticular pattern predominantly in the perihilar area with consolidation and diffuse ground-glass opacity in both lung fields (Figure 1B). In addition, hemodynamic evaluation and lung ultrasound showed no congestion and laboratory markers, including a procalcitonin level of 0.01 ng/mL, and ruled out an infectious etiology.

options.B: Discontinue amiodarone and administer a corticosteroid

answer: Discontinue amiodarone and administer a corticosteroid
explanation: B. Discontinue amiodarone and administer a corticosteroid As one of the antiarrhythmic drugs commonly used to treat ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias, amiodarone has complex pharmacology and has potential for significant adverse reactions. This drug has been associated with a variety of adverse events since it tends to accumulate in several organs, including the lungs, which could induce amiodarone pulmonary toxicity.1,2Many systemic adverse effects are related to pharmacokinetic properties and resulting tissue accumulation. Amiodarone organ toxicity usually occurs after long-term oral therapy and is rarely found in short-term intravenous therapy, especially during loading doses. Although the incidence of acute amiodarone-induced pulmonary toxicity (AIPT) is rare, the onset of its clinical manifestations is highly variable and can be an aggressive form of pulmonary disease. Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is the most common pattern of AIPT, usually represented by diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes.2The diagnosis of ARDS is based on the following clinical criteria: acute onset of symptoms (less than 1 week), absence of cardiac failure or fluid overload, moderate to severe impairment of oxygenation, and bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema on chest computed tomography. The alternative forms of interstitial lung disease and relevant alternative causes of ARDS should also be considered. The workup for acute AIPT should focus on ruling out sepsis, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism as alternative causes. All clinicians should be vigilant of this possibility since amiodarone is widely used. Discontinuation or dose reduction may resolve most of its adverse effects and the prognosis is good if there is early detection of AIPT. Lung biopsy could be an option, but is not recommended for severe cases.3It is associated with increased mortality and morbidity and this procedure does not contribute to the presumed diagnosis since there are no noticeable histopathological differences between suspected acute AIPT-associated ARDS and ARDS of alternative origins.4Although the total bronchoalveolar cell count may be increased in AIPT, no difference in the number of absolute lymphocytes was observed in patients without toxicity compared with other causes of interstitial pneumonitis.5In addition, testing plasma amiodarone levels is not helpful because amiodarone levels are not predictive nor diagnostic of pulmonary toxicity.6 Improvement in symptoms after amiodarone cessation helps to support the diagnosis.7Most diagnosed patients respond well to discontinuation of amiodarone and administration of a corticosteroid (usually for up to 4 to 12 months). Several case reports suggest that glucocorticoid therapy is associated with substantial improvement, even in severe cases.8Glucocorticoid therapy must be tapered over 2 to 6 months after the clinical response is evident unless there are signs and symptoms of recurrence.9 Chest radiography on the third day after discontinuation of amiodarone and corticosteroid treatment showed improvement in the lung pattern, thus supporting the diagnosis of interstitial pneumonitis. Treatment was continued with oral prednisone (1 mg per kilogram of body weight) for a week and then the dose was decreased by 10 mg weekly. A chest radiography at the end of corticosteroid treatment showed a normal lung pattern without pulmonary infiltrates (Figure 2).

caption: The fluoroscopy image of the patient at the time of dyspnea.
scenario: A woman in her mid-20s was evaluated for a history of dyspnea on exertion for 2 years. On physical examination, her pulse was 70 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg. The cardiovascular examination showed a loud S1, normal S2, and an opening snap along with a mid-diastolic, soft, rumbling murmur at the apex of the heart. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left atrial enlargement. The echocardiogram showed severe mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2with a mean (SD) gradient of 20 (4) mm Hg. There was no evidence of any subvalvular thickening, leaflet calcification, or mitral regurgitation. The patient was taken for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV). A 6F pigtail catheter was placed in the left ventricle via the right femoral artery. The interatrial septum was punctured using a Mullins sheath and Brockenbrough needle via the right femoral vein. Entry into the left atrium was made and confirmed with a dye injection. However, suddenly, the patient developed acute onset of dyspnea along with retrosternal chest pain. Her blood pressure at the time of the event was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96%. The catheter was pulled back into the right atrium, and chest fluoroscopy was performed (Figure;Video).

options.D: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position

answer: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position
explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.
