Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
scenario: A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

options.A: Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan
options.C: Order anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing

answer: Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan
distractors: Order anti-RNA polymerase III antibody testing
explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

caption: Multiple annular, pink papules and thin plaques with slight hyperpigmentation and desquamation on patient’s right arm, forearm, and palm.
scenario: A 2-month-old boy, born at 39 weeks 1 day of gestation via normal spontaneous vaginal delivery with normal newborn screening results presented with a 10-day history of rash. On presentation, his temperature was 37.0 °C (98.6 °F); blood pressure, 113/74 mm Hg; and heart rate, 132 beats/min. Skin examination showed multiple annular, pink papules and plaques with hyperpigmentation and desquamation on the scalp, palms, and soles (Figure 1). Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory testing revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (238 U/L [reference, 9-80 U/L]) (3.97 μkat/L [reference, 0.15-1.34 μkat/L]) and alanine aminotransferase (261 U/L [reference, 13-45 U/L]) (4.36 μkat/L [reference, 0.22-0.75 μkat/L). Results of testing for antinuclear antibody, anti-SSA, and anti-SSB were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Of note, his mother had a negative rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at 12 and 32 weeks of pregnancy and a negative HIV test at 12 weeks of pregnancy.

options.B: Biopsy a skin lesion for histopathological evaluation.
options.C: Perform RPR and Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother.

distractors: Apply 1% topical hydrocortisone cream twice daily for 1 week.
Biopsy a skin lesion for histopathological evaluation.
Send skin scrapings for potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation and fungal culture.
explanation: C. Perform RPR andTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination (TPPA) testing in the infant and mother. The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that characteristic rash on the palms, soles, and scalp, along with transaminitis and hepatosplenomegaly on physical examination and ultrasound, are consistent with congenital syphilis. Topical corticosteroids (choice A) are not appropriate treatment for undiagnosed rash in an infant. Skin biopsy (choice B) is invasive and not the preferred initial option. Transaminitis and hepatomegaly with rash are not characteristic of superficial fungal infection, so KOH preparation (choice D) is not indicated. Congenital syphilis, caused by the spirocheteT pallidum,is transmitted to the fetus through the placenta or through direct contact with lesions during delivery.1Cases of congenital syphilis in the US exceeded 3800 in 2023, a more than 10-fold increase over the prior decade.2Risk factors for congenital syphilis include inadequate prenatal care, younger maternal age, lower educational attainment, low family income, unstable housing, substance use disorder, and history of incarceration.3The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends screening all pregnant women for syphilis at their first prenatal visit and in the third trimester, with risk-based screening at the time of delivery. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommends universal testing 3 times in pregnancy.4-6All pregnant patients who test positive for syphilis should be treated immediately to decrease the risk of congenital syphilis.5,6 Approximately 55% of neonates with congenital syphilis are asymptomatic at birth; 31% of symptomatic cases are diagnosed after age 3 months.7Infants with early congenital syphilis (onset before age 2 years) may have bullous or mucocutaneous eruptions (40%), hepatobiliary dysfunction (33%-100%), anemia and thrombocytopenia (37%), and osteochondritis or periostitis on skeletal radiography (75%).8The classic skin rash (oval, copper-red macular or papular, often desquamating, lesions on the palms and soles or elsewhere on the body) is contagious due to presence of spirochetes in the lesions.9Up to 60% of symptomatic newborns develop neurosyphilis, which may present with seizures and/or cranial nerve palsies.8Approximately 40% of infants born to pregnant patients with untreated syphilis develop late congenital syphilis (onset after age 2 years), which may present with bony abnormalities (osteochondritis or periostitis), Hutchinson teeth (notched, widely spaced teeth), ocular abnormalities (interstitial keratitis, uveitis, chorioretinitis), and sensorineural hearing loss.8,9 The CDC stratifies patients with possible congenital syphilis into 4 categories: confirmed or highly probable, possible, less likely, and unlikely based on characteristic clinical findings and nontreponemal test results.5Because maternal nontreponemal antibodies passively cross the placenta, diagnosis of early congenital syphilis requires nontreponemal testing (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory [VDRL] or RPR) of the infant and mother, using the same assay. An infant titer of 4 or greater times the maternal titer confirms congenital syphilis.8,9Infants with physical findings (eg, characteristic rash) or an RPR titer more than 4-fold higher than the maternal titer should undergo testing with complete blood cell count, liver function tests, lumbar puncture and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and long-bone radiographs.5 The differential diagnosis of congenital syphilis includes impetigo, fungal infection, neonatal lupus erythematosus, and SCORTCH infections (syphilis, cytomegalovirus, other viruses [eg, HIV, hepatitis B, Zika, parvovirus, rubella, toxoplasmosis, chickenpox, herpes simplex]).10 For confirmed or highly probable cases of congenital syphilis, standard therapy consists of a 10-day course of intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G.5After treatment, neonates with congenital syphilis should undergo regular monitoring of symptoms and serologic testing every 3 months until their titers decline at least 4-fold from the peak titer.9 The infant’s RPR was reactive, with a titer of 1:2048 (8-fold higher than maternal RPR [1:256]). The infant’s TPPA test result was positive. Results of HIV testing of the infant and mother were negative. Skeletal radiographs showed metaphyseal destruction on the medial aspects of the bilateral proximal tibias (Figure 2). CSF analysis showed a leukocyte count of 23 cells/μL (reference, 0-20 cells/μL), protein level of 170.9 mg/dL (reference, 15-45 mg/dL), and a reactive VDRL (titer 1:8), consistent with neurosyphilis. Findings on cerebral ultrasound, ocular examination, and hearing assessment were normal. The patient received 50 000 IU/kg of aqueous crystalline penicillin G every 6 hours for 10 days. At 6-week follow up, the infant’s skin lesions had resolved, liver function test results normalized, and the bony radiographic abnormalities had resolved. No clinical sequelae such as hearing loss, visual disturbances, or developmental delays were observed. At 9-month follow-up, the infant’s RPR titer had decreased more than 4-fold, to 1:16.

scenario: A 72-year-old woman with a bioprosthetic aortic valve implanted 6 years prior to presentation was evaluated for fevers, malaise, and weight loss. Five months prior, she developed fevers and chills while visiting the island of Elba, where she consumed raw milk products. Two weeks after initial improvement, she developed intermittent night sweats, fevers up to 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), fatigue, and weight loss of 10 kg (22.05 lb). At presentation, her temperature was 37.8 °C (100 °F); heart rate, 71 beats/min; and blood pressure, 126/80 mm Hg. Physical examination was normal except for a grade 2 cardiac systolic ejection murmur. Laboratory findings revealed a normal complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and transaminase level. C-reactive protein level was 13 mg/L (reference, <5 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 50 mm/h (reference, <20 mm/h). Rheumatoid factor level was 68 U/mL (reference, <14 U/mL). Results ofTreponema pallidumparticle agglutination and HIV testing were negative. Two sets of blood cultures showed no growth after 7 days. Findings of chest and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans were normal. An initial electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min and first-degree atrioventricular block. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TEE) revealed a normally functioning bioprosthetic aortic valve without vegetations. A TEE (Figure 1) showed normal valvular function and a thickened aortic root. Results of serologic testing forBrucellaspp andBartonella henselaewere negative. Phase I and II IgG titers forCoxiella burnetiiwere ≥1:10 240 (reference, <1:40). Phase I IgM titer was 1:160 and phase II IgM titer was 1:320 (reference, <1:40).

answer: Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT
explanation: Coxiella burnetiiendocarditis (Q fever endocarditis) B. Order cardiac fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG PET)/CT The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that in a patient with positiveCoxiellaserology and a thickened aortic root on TEE, cardiac FDG PET/CT is highly sensitive and specific for diagnosis of prosthetic valve endocarditis.1Cardiac MRI (choice A) is not the first-line imaging study because it is less sensitive for detection of small cardiac vegetations than cardiac FDG PET/CT. Choice C is not recommended because aortography is an invasive test. Repeat TEE in 5-7 days (choice D) in a patient with suspected endocarditis is contraindicated because it would delay treatment. Q (“Query”) fever is a zoonotic disease caused by the intracellular gram-negative bacillusCoxiella burnetii. Infected animals such as domestic ungulates (goats, cows, and sheep)2,3shed the bacteria in their birth products, urine, and feces. Transmission to humans occurs through contaminated aerosols and direct contact with infected animals or consumption of raw milk products.3 Approximately 50% of people with acuteC burnetiiinfection develop symptoms3such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias lasting 1 to 2 weeks; approximately one-half relapse after 2 to 3 weeks with fever, fatigue, headaches, and dry cough. Chronic infection (eg, endocarditis, osteoarticular or vascular infection) develops in less than 5%; risk factors include valvulopathies, immunosuppression, and pregnancy.3,4In a study of 185 patients with Q fever endocarditis, 89% of patients had underlying valvulopathy, previous valve replacement, or prosthetic cardiac material, and only 11% had normal cardiac valves.5Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis can be challenging because symptoms are nonspecific and the organism does not grow on routine culture media. Serology is used to diagnose Q fever and distinguish between acute and chronic infections. Phase II IgG antibodies, which appear 14 to 21 days after initial infection, indicate acute infection and may persist for years. Phase I IgG antibodies, typically detected a median of 29 days after acute infection, are elevated in chronic infection.6 Diagnosis ofC burnetiiendocarditis is made based on the 2023 Duke–International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases criteria for infective endocarditis7and phase I IgG antibody titer greater than 1:800 or positive polymerase chain reaction assay of blood or tissue (eg, explanted heart valves).2,7,8TEE is the recommended initial imaging study3; if TEE is indeterminate, cardiac FDG PET/CT, which has a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 86.5% for prosthetic valve endocarditis,1should be performed. Q Fever endocarditis is treated with doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (200-600 mg/d) for at least 18 months for native valve endocarditis and 24 months for prosthetic valve endocarditis.2Treatment success is determined by monitoring antibody titers every 3 months.9Absence of a 4-fold decrease in IgG phase I antibody titers and persistence of IgM phase II antibodies after 1 year of therapy is associated with increased mortality rates.3Valve surgery is indicated for patients with acute heart failure, local complications (abscess, false aortic aneurysm, enlarging vegetations), bacterial resistance, or vegetations larger than 10 mm with associated embolic complications such as ischemic stroke.2,3,8 Treatment was initiated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/d) and hydroxychloroquine (600 mg/d). Cardiac FDG PET/CT demonstrated circumferentially increased metabolic activity in the area of the prosthetic valve, suggestive of aortic root abscess (Figure 2). The patient developed intermittent grade 2 AV block. Three weeks after initial presentation, she underwent cardiac aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve. No aortic root abscess was noted during surgery. Vegetations were detected on the explanted aortic valve, and polymerase chain reaction assay of the specimen was strongly positive forC burnetii(1 256 990 copies/mL). At 6-month follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic, C-reactive protein level was normal, andC burnetiiantibody titers had decreased to 1:5120 for phase I IgG and 1:640 for phase II IgG. Treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is planned for a duration of 24 months.2

scenario: A 34-year-old previously healthy woman taking no medications was hospitalized after experiencing two 45-minute episodes of right-sided headaches over 72 hours, associated with transient left upper extremity hemiparesis and left hand numbness. She reported no smoking, drug misuse, alcohol consumption, or head trauma. Her mother and aunt experienced an ischemic stroke at ages 60 and 50 years, respectively. At presentation, her temperature was 36.5 °C (97.7 °F); heart rate, 70 beats/min; and blood pressure, 120/65 mm Hg in both arms. She had left-sided hemiparesis, with 4/5 strength in her left upper and lower extremities, and left-sided hyperreflexia. Findings on examination of her cranial nerves, sensory examination, and coordination testing were unremarkable. Complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, liver function test results, and C-reactive protein level were within reference ranges. Results of a urine cannabinoid screen were negative, and an electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast brain computed tomography scan showed multiple right cortico-subcortical hypodensities, compatible with infarcts in the right junctional territories (border zone between the main cerebral arterial territories). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed subacute right frontoparietal infarcts on diffusion-weighted imaging and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) revealed bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries, more severe on the right and with extension to the middle cerebral artery (MCA) (Figure 1).

distractors: Administer intravenous heparin (18 U/kg/h after a loading dose of 80 U/kg)
Prescribe intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/d for 3 days)
explanation: B. Obtain digital subtraction angiography The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that a stroke in a young patient with bilateral narrowing of the terminal portion of the intracranial carotid arteries and a family history of stroke is highly suggestive of moyamoya disease. Intravenous heparin (choice A) is contraindicated because anticoagulation increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage in patients with moyamoya disease. Lumbar puncture (choice C) is not recommended because there are no clinical signs of infection. Choice D is not indicated because steroids are not effective treatment for moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease is a noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid artery (ICA), leading to fragile collateral vessel formation.1﻿Moyamoya(Japanese for “puff of smoke”) refers to the angiographic findings of this abnormal vascular network.2 Moyamoya disease occurs in 0.1 per 100 000 people worldwide, but the prevalence is substantially higher in East Asia, especially Japan (17.6 per 100 000).3Moyamoya disease is approximately 2-fold more common among females than males and has a bimodal age distribution (at 10 years and 30 to 50 years).4A family history of moyamoya disease is reported in 12% to 15% of patients with the disease.3 Underlying pathophysiological mechanisms are unknown but may involve alterations in genes involved in vascular development and angiogenesis, includingMMP,VEGF, andPDGFRB. TheRNF213p.R4810K gene variant increases the risk of moyamoya disease among East Asian patients.4 Patients with moyamoya disease may have intermittent transient ischemic attacks and strokes typically involving border zone areas or have hemorrhagic events (intracranial or intraventricular) due to rupture of fragile reticular vessels. Headaches affect 20% to 76.4% of patients, often with migraine-like features such as unilaterality and aura.5The differential diagnosis includes atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease, autoimmune conditions (eg, systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome), and infectious vasculopathies (eg, meningitis, cytomegalovirus infection). The diagnosis of moyamoya disease is made based on digital subtraction angiographic findings of (1) stenosis or occlusion of arteries in the terminal portion of the intracranial ICA and (2) abnormal vascular networks in the vicinity of the stenotic lesions. Brain MRI or MRA are less accurate for diagnosis, particularly in patients with unilateral lesions, those older than 60 years, or those with early-stage moyamoya disease.6 There is no curative treatment for moyamoya disease. Among patients presenting with ischemic events, surgical revascularization with a direct bypass (extracranial-intracranial anastomosis) or indirect bypass (eg, placement of superficial temporal artery onto the brain surface to promote new blood vessel growth) is associated with decreased risk of ischemic stroke and death. Patients receiving nonsurgical management of ischemic events have recurrent annual stroke rates of 20% to 50%.7 Asymptomatic patients with moyamoya disease have a 1.4% to 15% annual risk of stroke.7,8For these patients, bypass surgery is associated with a 26% reduction in the risk of death but a 76% increase in the risk of hemorrhagic events compared with nonsurgical management.7 Per 2021 Japanese guidelines, based on limited evidence (grade C), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, or cilostazol) can be considered to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with moyamoya disease and a history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack, those awaiting surgery, or those ineligible for surgery due to advanced age or comorbidities.9Endovascular treatment (angioplasty and/or stent) is associated with restenosis rates of 68.8%, and high rates (9.5%) of complications such as vessel rupture and intracerebral hemorrhage.10 Digital subtraction angiography revealed an abnormal net-like vascular network with a “smoke puff” appearance near the stenotic terminal portion of the ICA bilaterally (Figure 2and video). The patient received aspirin (75 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg). Seven days after initial presentation, she developed a new stroke and underwent an indirect bypass revascularization procedure. On postoperative day 21, she developed a right MCA ischemic stroke causing left hemiplegia. Two years later, she developed right-sided hemiparesis due to occlusion of the first segment of the left MCA and underwent direct bypass connecting the left superficial temporal artery to the left MCA. Four years after initial presentation, she has persistent left hemiparesis and a left steppage gait. Genetic testing revealed no pathogenic variants.

scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with a 7-year history of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, typically lasting 3 to 5 days and occurring approximately every 6 months. The pain was crampy and diffuse; accompanied by mild abdominal distension without nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or hematochezia; and not relieved by eating or defecation. She reported no past medical history, allergies, or use of prescription or illicit drugs. On presentation, her temperature was 36.7 °C (98.06 °F); blood pressure, 120/78 mm Hg; and heart rate, 97 beats/min. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding. She had mild, nonpitting painless swelling on the dorsum of both hands, accompanied by pruritus. Laboratory testing revealed normal hemoglobin level and normal liver and kidney function and urinalysis results. Serum complement C4 level was 5.31 mg/dL (reference, 14-36 mg/dL). Levels of antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin were normal. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) performed during an episode of abdominal pain showed jejunal wall edema and ascites (Figure 1). Gastroscopy, colonoscopy, and small bowel endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities. The patient reported that her father and brother experienced similar unexplained recurrent episodes of abdominal pain.

options.B: Check C1 inhibitor level and function

answer: Check C1 inhibitor level and function
distractors: Administer methylprednisolone (60 mg intravenously daily for 3 days)
Perform deep endoscopic biopsy of the small bowel
explanation: B. Check C1 inhibitor level and function The key to the diagnosis is recognizing that recurrent episodes of abdominal pain in a patient with decreased C4 levels, and several first-degree family members with similar symptoms, are suggestive of HAE. Choice A is incorrect because corticosteroids are not effective for treatment of HAE.1Genetic testing (choice C) is not required for diagnosis of HAE.2Deep endoscopic biopsy (choice D) is not recommended due to risk of perforation and low diagnostic yield in the absence of mucosal abnormalities. HAE is a rare disorder, affecting approximately 0.002% of the global population, primarily caused by C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) deficiency or C1-INH dysfunction due to Serpin Family G Member 1 (SERPING1) gene variants.1C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor involved in the coagulation and inflammatory pathways, and low C1-INH protein levels lead to excess bradykinin, causing angioedema.3Inadequate C1-INH function triggers activation of the classical complement pathway, resulting in reduced serum C4 levels.3 HAE is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, but 25% of patients have de novo gene variants.4HAE is classified into 3 types, with types I and II often called HAE-C1-INH.2Type I (85% of type I/II) involves decreased levels of plasma C1-INH protein and functional C1-INH.1Type II (15% of type I/II) exhibits normal or elevated C1-INH levels but decreased functional C1-INH levels.1Type III (5%-10% of all cases) involves gene variants in other components of the bradykinin pathway, such as factor XII and plasminogen.5 HAE is characterized by recurrent episodes (attacks) of nonpitting subcutaneous and submucosal swelling that may affect the gastrointestinal tract, face (lips and tongue), upper airway (larynx), extremities, and genitals.6Abdominal pain due to gastrointestinal mucosal edema occurs in up to 93% of patients, and concomitant symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.7Abdominal pain may be the sole manifestation of HAE and, when severe, may be misdiagnosed as an acute surgical condition such as intestinal obstruction.7Laryngeal edema is a life-threatening manifestation that occurs in approximately 0.9% of attacks.4Triggers for HAE attacks may include trauma (eg, injury, dental procedures, surgery), medications (eg, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, or hormone replacement therapy), febrile illness, stress, and fatigue.1 Diagnosis of HAE-C1-INH is made based on decreased levels of C1-INH plasma protein and functional C1-INH, typically measured with an enzyme immunoassay.2Because quantitative and functional C1-INH testing may not be universally available, C4 levels, which are typically low in patients with HAE-C1-INH, may be a useful screening test.1,2Abdominal CT, ultrasound, and endoscopy may detect characteristic findings of bowel wall edema. The diagnosis of HAE is often delayed, with an average time from symptom onset to diagnosis of 8.4 years in the US and 12.64 years in China.8 For treatment of acute attacks of HAE, guidelines recommend a single dose of intravenous C1-INH concentrate, subcutaneous icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or subcutaneous ecallantide (plasma kallikrein inhibitor [PKI]).1Additional doses can be given if symptoms worsen, persist, or recur.2First-line long-term prophylactic medications include subcutaneous C1-INH concentrate (60 IU/kg twice weekly), lanadelumab (subcutaneous PKI; 300 mg every 2-4 weeks), or berotralstat (oral PKI; 150 mg once daily).1Decisions about long-term prophylaxis should be individualized, accounting for factors such as attack frequency, severity, quality of life, and medication availability. With treatment, HAE attacks can resolve or be reduced, and patients with HAE have a normal life expectancy.1,9 The patient’s abdominal pain resolved spontaneously after 5 days. The diagnosis of type II HAE was made based on her normal plasma C1-INH protein level and markedly reduced C1-INH function (2% [reference, >68%]). Her father and brother also had normal C1-INH protein levels and reduced functional C1-INH (both <1%). Five months after initial presentation, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain, which resolved within 1 hour after administration of icatibant (30 mg subcutaneously). Genetic testing identified a missenseSERPING1variant (c.1397G>A), which has been reported in type II HAE.10Four months later, the patient reported no recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, and CT scan revealed no jejunal edema or ascites (Figure 2). She is not currently taking any medication for HAE but carries icatibant to treat an acute attack of HAE.

scenario: A 25-year-old woman with migraines for 10 years presented with palpitations, fatigue, and worsening migraines. Her heart rate was 93 beats/min and blood pressure was 120/92 mm Hg. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram results were normal. Subsequent 48-hour Holter monitoring showed sinus tachycardia with a mean heart rate of 108 beats/min. Metoprolol succinate (25 mg daily) was started. Six months later, she was admitted to the hospital with 1 day of fevers, nausea, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.7 °C (101.7 °F); heart rate, 103 beats/min; and blood pressure, 138/89 mm Hg. Abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a left anterior pararenal retroperitoneal mass. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without intravenous contrast showed a 4.0 × 3.5–cm T1 and T2 hypointense, enhancing infrarenal left para-aortic mass without local tissue or vascular invasion (Figure). Plasma normetanephrine concentration was 907 pg/mL (reference, 0-145 pg/mL) and plasma metanephrine concentration was within reference range.

options.D: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)

answer: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)
explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

scenario: A 34-year-old woman presented with 1 year of progressive skin tightening over her right elbow and forearm, bilateral forearm and anterior tibia pain, and difficulty extending her fingers and elbows. She had no history of autoimmune disease, diabetes, Raynaud phenomenon, or trauma, but her symptoms worsened after playing tennis. Six months prior, she received prednisone (40 mg daily for 3 days), which mildly improved her forearm and anterior tibia pain and decreased her skin tightening for several days. Physical examination revealed right forearm induration with linear depressions (Figure), hypopigmented plaque with violaceous borders over the right elbow, bilateral hand swelling, and skin tightening over the bilateral forearms and anterior tibia region. She had no digital pitting or skin tightening over her face or fingers. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:320 (reference, ≤1:80) with a speckled pattern, and results of an extractable nuclear antigen antibodies panel were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated increased signal of the superficial and deep myofascial planes in the extensor compartments of the forearm on fluid-sensitive, fat-saturated sequences.

explanation: C. Prescribe 40-mg prednisone daily for 14 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the presence of a linear depression along a superficial vein, visible when the forearm is raised, which is characteristic of eosinophilic fasciitis. Topical clobetasol (choice A) is incorrect because eosinophilic fasciitis consists of deeper fascial sclerosis that is not adequately treated by topical steroids.1,2High-dose immunoglobulin (choice B) and mycophenolate mofetil (choice D) are not first-line treatments for eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis is rare, with fewer than 600 reported cases worldwide, has no known etiology, and typically affects adults aged 30 to 60 years.4Patients initially develop subacute pain, erythema, and nonpitting edema of limbs or trunk that progresses to symmetric deep, woody skin induration over months to years.4Collagenous thickening of the subcutaneous fascia gives the skin an “orange peel” appearance.4Fibrosis and tethering of connective tissue around superficial veins cause the venous groove sign—a linear depression resulting from overlying epidermis being pulled inward along a vein.4 Eosinophilic fasciitis is associated with hematologic malignancies (eg, Hodgkin lymphoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, multiple myeloma), graft-vs-host disease, hemodialysis initiation, radiation therapy, and  sustained intense physical exertion such as running. Based on case reports and small case series, certain medications are associated with eosinophilic fasciitis, including immune checkpoint inhibitors (eg, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab), statins, and proton pump inhibitors (eg, esomeprazole, lansoprazole).3,5 The criterion standard for the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis is presence of dermal and fascial fibrosis with or without eosinophils on a wedge biopsy that includes skin, subcutaneous fat, and fascia.1However, in some cases the diagnosis may be made clinically in patients who have nonpitting edema or symmetric induration in distal limbs; MRI findings of fascial thickening with hyperintense T2 signal and contrast enhancement; and supportive but nonspecific laboratory findings, such as elevated inflammatory markers (eg, C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and hypergammaglobulinemia.4,6Prior to treatment with steroids, most patients initially have peripheral eosinophilia.3,7 The differential diagnosis includes systemic sclerosis, scleromyxedema and scleredema, and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (associated with consumption of L-tryptophan or 5-hydroxytryptophan supplements).4,8Patients with eosinophilic fasciitis have cutaneous fibrosis but lack other characteristic features of systemic sclerosis, including digital and facial skin sclerosis, nailfold capillary abnormalities, Raynaud phenomenon, visceral involvement (eg, esophageal dysfunction, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis), and specific autoantibodies such as antitopoisomerase I (Scl-70), anticentromere, anti-RNA polymerase III, and anti-U3-RNP (fibrillarin).4Differentiating eosinophilic fasciitis from systemic sclerosis is important because in patients with systemic sclerosis, steroids can trigger renal crisis, which involves a sudden-onset, severe increase in blood pressure and rapid decline in kidney function.9 First-line treatment for eosinophilic fasciitis is oral prednisone (0.5-1 mg/kg daily), although 3 days of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg) may be used in severe cases.7Steroid doses are tapered based on clinical response, and more than 70% of patients have complete resolution of cutaneous swelling after taking prednisone for several months, although the groove sign may persist several years after treatment.2,4Immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil may be added for extensive disease or to help taper or discontinue steroids.4,9,10Based on case series, tocilizumab, baricitinib, infliximab, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulins may be effective for severe eosinophilic fasciitis.3Physical therapy to prevent limb contractures is recommended for all patients with eosinophilic fasciitis.3 Eosinophilic fasciitis was diagnosed based on the patient’s history, venous groove sign, and characteristic findings on MRI. After 1 month of treatment with oral prednisone (40 mg daily), she gained 4.54 kg (10 lb), so oral methotrexate (20 mg weekly) with folic acid (1 mg daily) was initiated, and the prednisone dose was tapered over 3 months. She underwent physical therapy twice weekly and was advised to take oral calcium (1000 mg daily) and vitamin D (1000 IU daily) due to concerns about adverse effects on bone associated with steroid use and to use contraception due to potential teratogenicity of methotrexate. At most recent follow-up 6 months after initial presentation, the skin tightening on her bilateral forearms and shins had decreased and her hand and elbow mobility had improved, but the groove sign on the right forearm persisted.

caption: Patient's peripheral blood smears by hospital day, showing schistocytes (arrowheads) (Giemsa-Wright; original magnification ×100).
scenario: A 52-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with 3 days of headache, fatigue, and expressive aphasia. She did not take medications, supplements, or illicit substances. She was afebrile, with blood pressure of 232/133 mm Hg and heart rate of 86/min. She had expressive aphasia and confusion but no other neurologic abnormalities. Laboratory values included platelet count 35 000/μL (reference, 150 000-450 000/μL); haptoglobin level, 20 mg/dL (reference, 41-165 mg/dL); lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level, 962 U/L (16.07 μkat/L) (reference, 140-280 U/L [2.34-4.68 μkat/L]); creatinine level, 1.44 mg/dL (127.3 μmol/L) (reference, 0.6-1.1 mg/dL [53.04-97.24 μmol/L]); total bilirubin, 2.7 mg/dL (46.18 μmol/L) (reference, 0.1-1.2 mg/dL [1.71-20.52 μmol/L]); indirect bilirubin, 1.6 mg/dL (27.37 μmol/L) (reference, 0.2-0.8 mg/dL [3.42-13.68 μmol/L]); and fibrinogen, 420 mg/dL (reference, 200-400 mg/dL). Hemoglobin level, mean corpuscular volume, international normalized ratio, vitamin B12level, and thyrotropin level were normal. A peripheral blood smear showed 1 schistocyte per high-power field (Figure). PLASMIC score was 5, consistent with a 6% risk of immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP). A sample for disintegrin and metalloprotease with thrombospondin type 1 repeats-13 (ADAMTS13) activity was sent. Testing for HIV, CMV, HCV, Lyme ELISA, ANA, dsDNA, and Coombs test were normal. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain showed diffuse cerebral edema without ischemia or mass effect. She was treated with intravenous nicardipine for hypertensive emergency. Her blood pressure declined to 128/76 mm Hg and her expressive aphasia resolved, but she remained confused, with poor insight and diminished attention. On hospital day 4, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed numerous multifocal infarctions, ADAMTS13 activity was 6% (normal, ≥61%) with an inhibitor titer of 2.9 Bethesda units (reference, ≤0.4), and her peripheral blood smear showed 5 schistocytes per high-power field (Figure). Hemoglobin level was 9.3 g/dL; platelet count, 65 000 cells/μL; haptoglobin level, less than 20 mg/dL; and LDH level, 597 U/L (9.97 μkat/L).

options.A: Continue nicardipine to goal systolic blood pressure of less than 160 mm Hg
options.B: Start daily therapeutic plasma exchange and methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days
options.C: Initiate 4 sessions of weekly rituximab (375 mg/m2)

answer: Start daily therapeutic plasma exchange and methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days
distractors: Continue nicardipine to goal systolic blood pressure of less than 160 mm Hg
Initiate 4 sessions of weekly rituximab (375 mg/m2)
explanation: Immune thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP) B. Start daily therapeutic plasma exchange and methylprednisolone (1000 mg) for 3 days The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), increasing schistocytes on serial blood smears, diminished ADAMTS13 activity, and a high inhibitor titer are consistent with iTTP. Although the initial PLASMIC score suggested an intermediate probability of iTTP, therapeutic plasma exchange was not initiated due to a paucity of schistocytes on initial blood smear, and hypertensive emergency was a reasonable explanation for thrombotic microangiopathy. Choice A is incorrect because the hemolysis and altered mental status did not improve with blood pressure control. Rituximab (choice C) is not recommended as monotherapy for iTTP. Platelet transfusion (choice D) is contraindicated in iTTP because it can potentiate microvascular thrombosis and increase mortality. TTP is defined by reduced activity of ADAMTS13, an enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor (vWF), and is caused by immune dysfunction (iTTP) or pathogenic variants of theADAMTS13gene (congenital TTP). In iTTP, antibodies neutralize or increase clearance of ADAMTS13, thereby decreasing ADAMTS13 activity. ADAMTS13 activity less than 10% to 20% leads to formation of large vWF multimers, causing microvasculature thromboses, such as myocardial infarction and stroke.1 ADAMTS13 activity less than 10% in patients with thrombocytopenia and MAHA is diagnostic of TTP.1Decreased ADAMTS13 activity (10%-40% activity) without MAHA may occur in pregnancy, uremia, and inflammation (eg, severe sepsis, acute liver failure, multiple sclerosis, COVID-19). MAHA without decreased ADAMTS13 activity may occur with hypertensive emergency, disseminated intravascular coagulation, HELLP syndrome (preeclampsia, hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme levels, low platelet count), hemolytic uremic syndrome, and scleroderma renal crisis.2Obtaining results of ADAMTS13 activity testing typically takes several days. Therefore, the PLASMIC clinical prediction tool can guide decisions about initiating empirical treatment for iTTP. The PLASMIC score includes 7 laboratory values (platelet count, reticulocyte count, haptoglobin level, indirect bilirubin level, mean corpuscular volume, international normalized ratio, creatinine level) and ranges from 0 to 7, with scores 6 to 7 considered as indicating high risk of TTP.3 First-line therapy for iTTP includes therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids. Rituximab, a monoclonal antibody against CD20, is also recommended to reduce relapse rates,4although randomized trial data are lacking.5Caplacizumab, a humanized, bivalent immunoglobulin fragment, was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2019 for initial treatment of iTTP along with therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids. Adding caplacizumab to therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids reduces rates of refractory iTTP, exacerbations of iTTP, and treatment response time but does not improve survival.6-8However, caplacizumab is expensive and increases bleeding risk.9 A response to TTP therapy is defined as a platelet count greater than 150 000 cells/μL for 2 consecutive days and LDH level less than 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, without new or progressive ischemic organ injury.10Clinical remission is defined by absence of thrombocytopenia and hemolysis, clinical stability, and a sustained response for 30 days or longer or ADAMTS13 activity 20% or greater. On hospital day 4, after ADAMTS13 activity result was reported at 6%, the patient was treated with daily therapeutic plasma exchange and methylprednisolone (1000 mg daily) for 3 days, followed by methylprednisolone (65 mg daily) for 3 days, and prednisone (50 mg daily), which was tapered by 10 mg every 3 days. After 5 daily therapeutic plasma exchange sessions, her ADAMTS13 activity was 14% and platelet count was 173 000 cells/μL, and she declined further plasma exchange. Beginning on hospital day 18, the patient received 4 weekly infusions of rituximab (375 mg/m2). On hospital day 30, discharge medications included amlodipine, labetalol, and prednisone (30 mg daily); platelet count was 191 000 cells/μL, and hemoglobin level was 13.2 g/dL. Approximately 1.5 years after initial presentation, the patient appeared well and was not taking iTTP-directed therapy. Platelet count was 220 000 cells/μL and ADAMTS13 activity was 66% without a detectable inhibitor.

caption: Facial swelling (left), chest imaging (center) showing pneumomediastinum, and computed tomography (right) showing air in the subcutaneous tissues of the face and neck.
scenario: A 37-year-old woman with no history of lung disease experienced sudden-onset tearing pain in her jaw several minutes into a routine dental cleaning procedure performed with a high-pressure stream of water, air, and cleaning powder. She then developed swelling of her face, neck, and chest and experienced chest tightness. She was treated immediately with pheniramine (45.5 mg intravenously) and methylprednisolone (80 mg intravenously), but the swelling in her face, neck, and chest increased, and she developed dyspnea and chest pain. She was transferred to an emergency department, where her blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg; pulse rate, 130/min; respiration, 25/min; and oxygen saturation, 92% while breathing room air. Physical examination revealed facial swelling (Figure) and palpable subcutaneous crepitus over her anterior chest wall, neck, and periorbital region. She received oxygen via a face mask at a rate of 6 L/min and intravenous dexamethasone (8 mg), intravenous acetaminophen (paracetamol) (1000 mg), and nebulized ipratropium bromide (0.5 mg), salbutamol (2.5 mg), and budesonide (1 g). Chest radiography and computed tomography showed air located in the subcutaneous tissues of the face and neck (Figure) and in the fascial planes of the neck and mediastinum.

options.B: Evaluate for endobronchial injury with emergency bronchoscopy
options.C: Initiate surgical decompression with mediastinal drainage

distractors: Evaluate for endobronchial injury with emergency bronchoscopy
Initiate surgical decompression with mediastinal drainage
explanation: A. Administer high-flow oxygen therapy The key to the correct answer is recognizing that pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema are typically self-limited conditions that may resolve more rapidly with oxygen therapy. Bronchoscopy (choice B) is not recommended because the patient had no evidence of major airway trauma. Choice C is incorrect because mediastinal drainage is reserved for airway perforation, esophageal rupture, or severe progressive respiratory distress. Needle decompression (choice D) is not indicated because the patient did not have a tension pneumothorax. Pneumomediastinum is defined as presence of free air within the mediastinal space and may occur spontaneously or secondary to trauma, procedures (eg, bronchoscopy, endoscopy, dental procedures, head and neck operations),1,2pulmonary disease (eg, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease), and infection (eg, pertussis, tuberculosis,Mycoplasma pneumoniae, COVID-19, influenza).2Spontaneous pneumomediastinum is associated with activities that increase intrathoracic pressure, such as smoking and vaping, and inhalational use of hookah, cocaine, and methamphetamine.2Sudden changes in intrathoracic pressure due to coughing, sneezing, vomiting, and strenuous physical exertion can precipitate pneumomediastinum, especially in patients with pulmonary disease.2High-pressure dental airflow devices, including air-powder polishers, high-speed drills, and air-water syringes, generate strong jets of air and water that can track into subcutaneous and mediastinal tissues through small defects in the gingival or mucosal surfaces, causing pneumomediastinum.3 The incidence of pneumomediastinum due to dental air and water flow devices is rare.1Case series report that patients at higher risk include those undergoing prolonged dental procedures with air-driven tools, individuals with chronic corticosteroid use or connective tissue disorders, and those undergoing mandibular third molar extraction.1Additionally, directing high-pressure air into gingival pockets or open wounds increases the risk of air dissection into the mediastinum.1 Patients with pneumomediastinum typically present with chest pain, dyspnea, and neck pain. Subcutaneous emphysema occurs in approximately 35%2of patients with pneumomediastinum. Hamman sign—a crunching or bubbling sound heard during cardiac auscultation—is identified in 5.9% of patients with pneumomediastinum, and concurrent pneumothorax occurs in approximately 5.2%.2,3 Although the initial diagnostic imaging study is typically a chest radiograph, its sensitivity for identifying pneumomediastinum ranges from 61% to 100%.4Chest computed tomography, the criterion standard, should be obtained in patients clinically suspected of having pneumomediastinum that is not identified on chest radiograph.5 Pneumomediastinum is typically self-limited with conservative management. However, high-flow oxygen therapy can enhance resorption of mediastinal air3by increasing the alveolar partial pressure of oxygen, creating a diffusion gradient that promotes the displacement of nitrogen from the mediastinal air pocket, leading to faster resolution of pneumomediastinum. Additionally, supportive care, including analgesia, bed rest, and avoidance of activities that increase intrathoracic pressure (eg, forced coughing or heavy lifting) for 1 week, is recommended.5Daily chest imaging should be performed to ensure that pneumomediastinum is resolving. Rare complications of pneumomediastinum include tension pneumomediastinum, mediastinitis, pneumoperitoneum, pneumopericardium, and pneumorrhachis (air within the spinal canal). Tension pneumomediastinum occurs if increased air pressure within the mediastinum compresses the trachea and major blood vessels, reducing venous return and decreasing cardiac output. Treatment involves immediate decompression of the mediastinum with needle aspiration, placement of a chest tube, or surgery (emergent anterior subxiphoid incision).2,5-7Mediastinitis typically presents with fever, increased chest pain, and odynophagia and is treated with thoracoscopic drainage and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Patients with pneumomediastinum should be hospitalized for close monitoring and supportive care if they have chest pain, respiratory distress, hemodynamic instability, hypoxemia, rapidly worsening subcutaneous emphysema, tension pneumomediastinum, pneumomediastinum with lung disease (eg, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma), or suspected esophageal perforation. Patients with mild, stable pneumomediastinum based on clinical findings and vital signs may be discharged from the emergency department with follow-up evaluation in 24 to 48 hours.5,8,9 The patient was admitted to the thoracic surgical service and received oxygen by nasal cannula (6 L/min) and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory analgesia (dexketoprofen [50 mg/2 mL], intramuscularly twice daily). Daily chest radiography demonstrated a gradual decrease in pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema. On hospital day 4, she was asymptomatic and was discharged. Two months after discharge, her chest radiograph was normal. The patient was advised to avoid high-pressure air and water devices during future dental cleanings to reduce the risk of recurrent pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema.

caption: Left, Crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous lesions on patient’s face. Right, Ulcerative lesions on back.
scenario: A 25-year-old man taking no regular medications presented to clinic with a 1-month history of skin lesions, which began as small painless papules on his face and progressed to vesicles and pustules over 1 week. Two weeks prior to presentation, he received empirical treatment for herpes simplex virus with a 7-day course of acyclovir (400 mg 3 times daily). However, the lesions enlarged, became verrucous, and new ulcerated, papular lesions appeared on his trunk and extremities; he developed fevers to 39 °C (102.2 °F) and malaise. He had no known history of sexually transmitted infections but reported unprotected sex with multiple male partners. He reported recent exposure to a work colleague with active tuberculosis. At presentation, temperature was 37.4 °C (99.3 °F); respirations, 18/min; heart rate, 80/min; and blood pressure, 102/64 mm Hg; oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination revealed crusted, ulcerative, pustular, nodular, and verrucous facial lesions, ulcerative lesions on his back and limbs, and papular lesions across his body (Figure). He had no mucosal lesions or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory results revealed normal hemoglobin level, white blood cell count, glucose level, and liver function. A fourth-generation immunoassay test for HIV was positive, CD4 count was 125 cells/mm3, and HIV viral load was 157 000 copies/mL. A fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) result was positive. Results of tests for rapid plasma reagin (RPR), human T-lymphotropic virus 1, and tuberculin purified protein derivative were negative. Bacterial culture of the skin lesions grew methicillin-resistantStaphylococcus aureus. Fungal and mycobacterial cultures of the skin lesions were negative, and chest radiography findings were normal.

options.B: Repeat the RPR test with dilution
options.C: Send an interferon gamma release assay
options.D: Start vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours)

answer: Repeat the RPR test with dilution
distractors: Send an interferon gamma release assay
Start vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours)
explanation: B. Repeat the RPR test with dilution The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that despite the negative RPR test result, the patient’s symptoms, sexual history, positive HIV test result, and positive FTA-ABS result are highly suggestive of syphilis. Skin biopsy (choice A) can provide valuable histopathological information but is invasive and not the first option. Interferon gamma release assay (choice C) is not the appropriate test to diagnose active tuberculosis. Vancomycin (choice D) is incorrect because treatment of methicillin-resistantS aureusfrom a superficial skin culture is not indicated. Malignant syphilis, caused by the spirocheteTreponema pallidum,is a rare and severe form of secondary syphilis characterized by disseminated ulcerative lesions and often accompanied by systemic symptoms of fever, malaise, arthralgias, and myalgias. Skin lesions typically begin as papules and progress to pustules and then to ulcerated, crusted lesions, often with a necrotic center.1Malignant syphilis is more common with immunocompromised conditions such as HIV, use of immunotherapy, malnutrition, diabetes, and alcohol use disorder.2A study of 11 368 HIV-infected patients reported that 1% had syphilis; of those, 7.3% had malignant syphilis.3Histopathology of skin lesions reveals a dense inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrating spirochetes in tissue occurs in approximately 57% of malignant syphilis cases.4 The differential diagnosis of malignant syphilis includes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis; progressive disseminated histoplasmosis; cryptococcosis, mpox, mycosis fungoides, and tuberculosis verrucosa cutis. There are 2 algorithms to diagnose syphilis, and the choice of algorithm depends on the availability and cost of testing and level of endemicity.5,6The initial test in the reverse algorithm is a treponemal test (eg, FTA-ABS), which detects specific antibodies againstT pallidumand provides a qualitative result (reactive or nonreactive).5,6Because these antibodies can persist lifelong, a positive treponemal test result does not differentiate between newly acquired and previously treated syphilis infection and should be confirmed with a nontreponemal test (eg, RPR or venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL] test). The initial test in the traditional algorithm is a nontreponemal test that assesses serum reactivity to a lecithin-cholesterol-cardiolipin antigen to identify IgG and IgM antibodies in individuals infected withT pallidum.Nontreponemal tests provide semiquantitative results, and the amount of IgM and IgG antibodies reflects the activity of syphilitic infection.5A positive nontreponemal test result should be followed by confirmatory testing with a treponemal test. A nontreponemal test result may be falsely negative when very high syphilis antibody titers interfere with formation of antigen-antibody complex lattice, thereby preventing visible agglutination.7This phenomenon, called the prozone effect, occurs more frequently in patients with HIV, likely due to B-cell dysregulation causing high antibody levels.7When the prozone effect is suspected, the RPR test should be repeated with dilution. Malignant syphilis is treated as secondary syphilis, with a single dose of 2.4 million units of intramuscular benzathine penicillin.8Response to therapy is defined as at least a 4-fold decrease in RPR titer at 12 months,9with rapid disappearance of systemic symptoms and resolution of skin lesions. To evaluate for the prozone effect, a repeat RPR test with dilution was performed and was reactive, with a titer greater than 1:128. A lumbar puncture, performed to rule out neurosyphilis, revealed normal cerebrospinal fluid findings, and the fluid tested negative on VDRL test. Findings on fundoscopic examination to evaluate for ocular syphilis were unremarkable. The patient received a single intramuscular dose of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin and started antiretroviral treatment for HIV with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. His skin lesions improved over 2 weeks and resolved after 1 month. At 1 year after therapy, RPR had decreased to 1:8. At most recent follow-up, 24 months after initial presentation, the patient was taking antiretroviral treatment, his CD4 count was 383 cells/mm3, and viral load was undetectable (<40 copies/mL). Skin examination revealed areas of residual postinflammatory hyperpigmentation on his face.

scenario: A 58-year-old woman with no history of allergies or rheumatic disease presented to the allergy clinic with a 2-year history of spontaneous wheals that occurred daily, accompanied by pruritus and a burning sensation (Figure). The wheals typically appeared in the evening, persisted for several hours, and resolved without residual hyperpigmentation or bruising. For the past 2 years, she experienced daily fatigue, arthralgia (hands, feet, shoulders, and knees), myalgia (arms and legs), intermittent fevers (>38.5 °C [101.3 °F] in some episodes), and chills 2 to 3 times per week. Six months prior to presentation, results of a complete blood cell count were normal, and her C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 7.6 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). At symptom onset, a dermatologist diagnosed chronic spontaneous urticaria, which was treated with several second-generation H1antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, and fexofenadine) at up to 4-fold standard doses daily for several weeks. Although her symptoms did not improve with antihistamines, treatment with high-dose glucocorticoids (2 separate 1-month duration prednisolone [40 mg] treatments, in which prednisolone dose was tapered by 5 mg every week) resolved the wheals, fatigue, arthralgia, myalgia, and fever. However, symptoms recurred after discontinuation of glucocorticoids. Physical examination revealed wheals on the entire body, excluding the face, palms, soles, and genital area. She had no mucosal involvement, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly and no joint swelling. Her CRP level was 20.9 mg/L (reference, 0-5 mg/L). Results of complete blood cell count, creatinine level, and liver function tests were normal. Results of tests for double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and an extractable nuclear antigen screen were normal. A skin biopsy sample showed dense dermal infiltration of neutrophils, without blood vessel infiltration and inflammation.

options.A: Order an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay blood test for Lyme disease
options.C: Start penicillin VK (500 mg orally 4 times a day for 10 days)
options.D: Treat with methotrexate (15 mg subcutaneously once a week for 3-6 months)

distractors: Order an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay blood test for Lyme disease
Start penicillin VK (500 mg orally 4 times a day for 10 days)
Treat with methotrexate (15 mg subcutaneously once a week for 3-6 months)
explanation: The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that chronic recurrent wheals that do not resolve with antihistamines, along with fever, arthralgia, elevated CRP level, and neutrophilic infiltrate on skin biopsy are characteristic of Schnitzler syndrome. A test for Lyme disease (choice A) is not recommended because diffuse wheals are not characteristic of Lyme disease. Antibiotics (choice C) are not indicated because the patient’s symptoms were not consistent with a skin infection. There was no evidence of vasculitis on skin biopsy, so treatment with methotrexate (choice D) is not indicated. Schnitzler syndrome is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disease of unknown etiology, with approximately 350 case reports published worldwide.1-3Wheals are typically the presenting symptom of Schnitzler syndrome.1,2Other common symptoms are fever (72%), joint pain (68%), and bone pain (55%).1Schnitzler syndrome is estimated to affect less than 1% of individuals with chronic urticaria and up to 1.5% of patients with monoclonal IgM gammopathy.4The median age of onset is 51 years, with a male to female ratio of 1.5.1 Schnitzler syndrome is diagnosed based on presence of 2 major criteria: chronic urticarial rash (wheals) and a monoclonal IgM (85%) or IgG (7%) gammopathy, although isolated IgA monoclonal gammopathy has been recently described.1,2,5In addition, the diagnosis requires presence of least 2 minor criteria (with IgM monoclonal gammopathy) or 3 minor criteria (with IgG monoclonal gammopathy), including recurrent unexplained fever, leukocytosis, and/or elevated CRP level, a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate on skin biopsy, or findings of abnormal bone remodeling (based on bone scintigraphy, magnetic resonance imaging, or elevated bone alkaline phosphatase level on blood testing).6 Schnitzler syndrome is likely underdiagnosed, and there is an average diagnostic delay of 3.3 years after onset of symptoms.2The differential diagnosis of Schnitzler syndrome includes chronic spontaneous urticaria,7urticarial vasculitis, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, adult-onset Still disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus. Antihistamines, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, and oral glucocorticoids typically have limited efficacy for patients with Schnitzler syndrome and may be associated with long-term adverse effects. However, treatment with IL-1/IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept, and canakinumab) is effective, although none of these treatments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for Schnitzler syndrome.1,2,8,9A systematic review of 7 studies (34 patients) reported that canakinumab treatment was associated with a complete response in 58.6% and a partial response in all remaining patients over a cumulative follow-up of 253 months.9The most common adverse event was infection (n = 79).9A 4-year follow-up study of 17 patients with Schnitzler syndrome reported long-term benefits of canakinumab, with most patients having no, minimal, or mild residual symptoms.8 Patients with Schnitzler syndrome, similar to those with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance,10are at increased risk of hematologic malignancies. In a study of 281 patients with Schnitzler syndrome, over a median follow-up of 8 years, 12% developed a hematologic malignancy; of these malignancies, 60% were Waldenström macroglobulinemia.1 A monoclonal gammopathy of the IgA type lambda was detected in a serum immunofixation test. Findings on bone marrow biopsy were normal. Results of hepatitis B and C antibody testing, interferon-gamma release assay, and HIV serology were negative. Treatment with anakinra (100 mg subcutaneously daily) resulted in resolution of the fever and wheals, but the patient’s arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue persisted. After 9 months, anakinra was stopped and canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks) was started. At her most recent visit, 46 months after presentation, the patient had no wheals, fever, or myalgia and only mild intermittent arthralgia in her right shoulder while taking canakinumab (300 mg every 6 weeks). Results of complete blood cell count with differential, serum immunofixation test, and free light chain ratio have remained unchanged and will continue to be checked every 6 months to screen for lymphoproliferative disorders.
