However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

caption: Top left (looking right and up), middle left (looking right), bottom left (looking right and down), center (primary position), top right (looking left and up), middle right (looking left), and bottom right (looking left and down). The images demonstrate left-eye hypotropia and left-eyelid ptosis at the primary position and impaired left-eye supraduction worse at lateral gaze on extraocular movements.
scenario: A 37-year-old Asian nonsmoking man with no known medical or drug history presented with an insidious onset of left-eye ptosis (only brought to attention by his friends on review of recent photographs) and subsequent painless vertical diplopia for 1 year. He did not complain of headaches, facial numbness, dysarthria, facial droop, dysphagia, or limb weakness or numbness. There was no history of joint pain or constitutional symptoms. Neurological examination revealed a nonfatigable partial left-eyelid ptosis, left-eye hypotropia at primary position, and impaired left eye supraduction (Figure 1) with a nonreactive left pupil on direct and consensual light reflexes. There were no other cranial nerve deficits. Limb reflexes, motor testing, and sensory testing results were normal, and the plantar responses were flexor. Laboratory evaluation showed a normal fasting serum glucose level, thyroid function test result, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Anti–double-stranded DNA, antinuclear antibodies, and HIV test results were negative. Repetitive nerve stimulation did not show any decremental response and anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies were negative. A computed tomography (CT) angiography of the circle of Willis did not show any aneurysms and a routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain did not show any infarcts or masses. Lumbar puncture was acellular with normal glucose and protein levels, and multiple microbiological test results were negative.

options.C: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm that is not picked up on CT angiography
options.D: Neurovascular conflict of the oculomotor nerve

answer: Neurovascular conflict of the oculomotor nerve
distractors: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm that is not picked up on CT angiography
explanation: D. Neurovascular conflict of the oculomotor nerve Further detailed MRI constructive interference in steady-state sequence with fine cuts of the midbrain was performed, which revealed that the left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and left superior cerebellar artery (SCA) were indenting the oculomotor nerve with resultant displacement (Figure 2). No intracranial aneurysms were demonstrated. An oculomotor nerve palsy with pupil involvement is often due to extrinsic compression by posterior communicating artery (PCoA) aneurysms.1This is because when the nerve exits the midbrain, its cisternal course2passes between the PCA and SCA and is accompanied by the PCoA before running in an anteromedial-lateral direction to reach the cavernous sinus. The dilated pupil occurs as external compression affects the pial vessels, which then compromise the parasympathetic fibers and results in paralysis of the sphincter pupillae. Compared with the more familiar neurovascular compression syndromes of trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasms,3nonaneurysmal neurovascular conflict causing oculomotor nerve palsy is not common.4However, high-resolution thin-sliced MRI has been found to be increasingly accurate in identifying and correlating symptoms with the extent of neurovascular compression,5and thus should remain a differential diagnosis.6This is of clinical significance, as cases with extensive negative workup are often labeled as idiopathic or attributed to microvascular causes,7which are conservatively managed with observation, whereas the treatment options of neurovascular conflict causing oculomotor nerve palsy ranges from the use of steroids to microvascular decompression.8 In this patient, in view of his significant symptoms with chronic persistent presentation, he underwent microvascular decompression  with significant improvement of the ptosis and ophthalmoparesis. This case emphasizes the importance of high-resolution MRI to look for neurovascular conflict in oculomotor nerve palsy with pupillary involvement, especially when no other cause has been found.

caption: A, The patient’s bilateral palms and fingers could not make full contact due to the limited mobility of interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints. B, Linear depression (arrowheads) was seen along the course of superficial vein when limb was elevated.
scenario: A 31-year-old man with insidious onset of limited mobility of joints visited our clinic for evaluation. Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). No muscular atrophy or sclerodactyly was found. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed. Blood test results indicated eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count, 1300 μL; reference, <500μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 31 mm/h; reference, <15 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP, 3.01 mg/dL; reference, <0.8 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.
explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

caption: Extraocular movements on presentation. Examination reveals deficits in elevation and abduction of both eyes not conforming to a cranial nerve distribution.
scenario: A 75-year-old woman presented with horizontal binocular diplopia, right-sided ptosis, and a new headache that was progressive over 3 days. She reported difficulty opening her jaw, pain when chewing, and a 2.3-kg weight loss. The week prior, she experienced left-sided ptosis that persisted for 2 days and subsequently resolved. She denied vision changes, eye pain, scalp tenderness, and myalgias. Past medical history included schizophrenia, hypothyroidism, and supraventricular tachycardia. Her examination demonstrated normal visual acuity in both eyes. Pupils were equal, round, and reactive. There was right upper-eyelid ptosis. Extraocular motility demonstrated limitation of elevation and abduction bilaterally (Figure 1). Results of dilated fundus examination were normal, and the remainder of her neurologic examination results were normal. Her eye movements and ptosis did not change with fatiguability, rest, or an ice-pack test. Investigations revealed a C-reactive protein level of 292 mg/L (normal, <10 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 93 mm/h (normal, <30 mm/h). A lumbar puncture demonstrated normal opening pressure, cell count, and glucose and protein levels. Magnetic resonance imaging with contrast of the brain demonstrated diffuse edema and enhancement of the scalp, skull base, neck, and paraspinal soft tissues, as well as T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of the extraocular muscles bilaterally. An additional test was obtained, and a diagnosis was made.
explanation: Facial and extraocular muscles are typically spared by the myositis associated with aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetase antibodies, and the lack of other features of antisynthetase syndrome (interstitial lung disease, nonerosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon) makes this diagnosis less likely. Immunoglobulin G4–related disease can cause enlargement of the extraocular muscles, creating a restrictive pattern of motility but may also be accompanied by hypertrophic pachymeningitis and sclerosing lesions of the abdomen and lungs. Lastly, although the history of transient contralateral ptosis may be reminiscent of myasthenia gravis, the lack of fatiguability, normal ice-pack test results, and soft tissue changes on magnetic resonance imaging suggest an alternate etiology. Temporal artery biopsy was obtained demonstrating intimal hyperplasia and transmural inflammation with giant cells (Figure 2), consistent with giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is classically thought to affect large and medium-sized arteries, although recent definitions reflect the capacity of GCA to affect vessels of any size.1Most patients with ocular GCA present with acute vision loss, with 80% attributable to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy owing to ischemia of the posterior ciliary arteries.2 Case series of GCA have demonstrated that although approximately 5% to 15% of patients report diplopia, only a subset have demonstrable oculomotor deficits on presentation, suggesting that ophthalmoplegia may be transient and underreported.2-4There are 2 proposed pathophysiologic mechanisms for ophthalmoplegia in GCA. The first is arteritic involvement of the vasa nervorum of the ocular motor nerves. However, ocular motility deficits in GCA often do not conform to the pattern of a cranial nerve. The second is arteritis of the vascular supply of the extraocular muscles. Despite the rich anastomotic vasculature from both the ophthalmic artery and branches of the external carotid artery, ischemia of the extraocular muscles has been observed. A histopathologic survey of the entire ocular motor apparatus in a case of GCA with severe ophthalmoparesis demonstrated extraocular muscle ischemia with preservation of cranial nerves 3, 4, and 6 along their entire course from the nerve nuclei to the orbits.5 Ptosis associated with ophthalmoplegia in GCA may be attributable to similar mechanisms.4Ptosis has also been reported in relation to Horner syndrome secondary to vasculitis affecting the vasa nervorum supplying the sympathetic plexus or direct granulomatous involvement of the sympathetic nerve fibers as they run alongside the inflamed vessel wall of the cavernous internal carotid artery.6,7 This patient had ocular motility deficits and ptosis that did not conform to the pattern of the ocular motor nerves and had no other signs of Horner syndrome. There was no ataxia or hemiparesis on examination, and magnetic resonance imaging ruled out a brainstem infarct. Her presentation was most suggestive of vasculitis leading to ischemia of the periorbital musculature. The patient promptly received high-dose intravenous steroids, which led to symptomatic improvement within hours. This case demonstrates the multifaceted presentation of GCA and the importance of maintaining a high suspicion in patients with elevated inflammatory markers, headache, and uncommon neuro-ophthalmic symptoms. When ocular motility abnormalities do not correspond to a typical ocular motor nerve palsy, ischemic myopathy should be considered, and prompt treatment with corticosteroids should be initiated to prevent vision loss and complications from GCA.

caption: T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging with gadolinium demonstrating thickening of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5; yellow arrowhead) at the level of Meckel cave and cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7; white arrowhead) in the internal auditory canal.
scenario: A 78-year-old man with a history of nonmelanoma skin cancers (NMSCs), including a left temporal skin cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) treated with cryosurgery, presented to primary care with left-sided upper and lower facial weakness diagnosed as Bell palsy. Eighteen months prior, he first became symptomatic with left external auditory canal dysesthesia. He was initially prescribed a neomycin sulfate, polymyxin b sulfate, and hydrocortisone solution that did not improve his left ear aches. Thereafter, the patient gradually developed a patch of numbness on the skin overlying the left tragus. One month prior to his initial visit, this sensory deficit had spread to the entire left half of his face and motor weaknesses emerged including diplopia and a left facial droop. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain studies at initial presentation and 2 months later noted stable periventricular and subcortical leukoencephalopathy favored to be microvascular ischemia that is common in older adults. Five months after the initial presentation, the patient had left-sided acute hearing loss, at which point a repeat brain MRI identified asymmetric thickening and enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve (CN5) extending to the cavernous sinus and the left facial nerve (CN7) extending to the internal auditory canal (Figure), with a differential of malignancy, infection, or inflammation. He was given a 3-week course of prednisone, 80 mg, by mouth once daily without noticeable benefit and referred to a tertiary care center for further evaluation.
explanation: Seven months after initial presentation, findings of a lumbar puncture were normal with no malignant cells identified, and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoproliferative disorder. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography found no distinct hypermetabolism. Serum studies indicated mildly elevated IgG4, beta-2-microglobulin, and lactate dehydrogenase. A computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the V3 branch of CN5 confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with positive pan-keratin and p40 staining. Next-generation sequencing showed a high tumor mutation burden (109.4 mutations/Mb) and many C>T/G>A and CC>TT/GG>AA substitutions at dipyrimidine sites. This mutational signature is typically associated with UV-induced DNA damage, suggesting an SCC of cutaneous rather than mucosal head and neck origin.1The patient was diagnosed with recurrent cSCC with perineural tumor spread (PNTS), which was surgically unresectable and unsuitable for curative-intent radiotherapy due to extensive involvement of CN5 and CN7. NMSCs are the most common cancers in the US, with cSCC having the highest incidence after basal cell carcinoma. Mohs surgery or other forms of excision with circumferential deep and peripheral margin assessment are considered the standard of care. Cryosurgery is not considered a standard treatment of cSCC. While most cSCCs are cured by surgery, a subset spreads along nerves. Perineural invasion (PNI) is microscopic cancer spread into nerves, seen in less than 15% of cSCC cases. More extensive PNI, involving large-caliber or cranial nerves, carries a higher risk of metastasis and mortality.2PNTS refers to the radiographic and clinical manifestations of PNI. This case initially presented as trigeminal neuralgia and facial paralysis diagnosed as Bell palsy but was later found to be PNTS from recurrent cSCC. PNTS from cSCC often involves CN5 and CN7, mimicking benign facial numbness and weakness. The concurrence of CN5 and CN7 deficits in patients with a history of NMSC should raise suspicion for PNTS. Tumor spread between these nerves occurs at specific sites, including the sphenopalatine ganglion, the lingual nerve-chorda tympani junction, and the auriculotemporal nerve.3The auriculotemporal nerve, a V3 branch, connects to CN7 in the retromandibular region and supplies sensation to the preauricular skin and external ear, explaining this patient’s symptoms. For cSCC unsuitable for curative surgery or radiation, anti–programmed cell death 1 protein checkpoint inhibitors are the standard of care, offering high response rates.4This patient received cemiplimab for 6 months, showing radiographic tumor regression without major immune-related adverse effects but persistent neuropathies, including complete left facial weakness. Facial reanimation surgery was performed to restore facial movements. Consolidation radiation therapy to residual disease along CN5 and CN7 was recommended alongside maintenance immunotherapy. PNTS to cranial nerves can be misdiagnosed as Bell palsy, a term often used for postviral neuropathies. However, PNTS should be considered in patients with a history of facial or scalp premalignant or malignant lesions, especially if symptoms persist or worsen despite corticosteroids. One review reported a median 6-month delay from symptom onset to diagnosis.5Timely referral to specialized centers is critical. MRI protocols optimized for cranial nerve imaging are essential for diagnosis, as early PNTS may be radiographically occult. Serial MRIs and targeted nerve biopsies help confirm the diagnosis, though biopsies may not always be feasible. Awareness of cSCC’s potential spread to CN5 and CN7 is vital for early detection and treatment, preventing diagnostic delays.

caption: Tongue lesions are shown.
scenario: A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).
explanation: The diagnosis of geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) is supported by the characteristic appearance of the tongue lesions as minimally symptomatic, well-demarcated, erythematous patches with hyperkeratotic borders in the absence of other cutaneous findings. The lesions may appear alarming, particularly in the context of cancer treatment, but are typically harmless. They frequently do not require intervention although topical analgesics can be offered to patients who are symptomatic. The patchy tongue lesions are inconsistent with the diffuse erythema of pellagra-associated glossitis (choice A), and the patient lacks the hallmark pellagra triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. While oral mucositis associated with cabozantinib is a consideration—the incidence of any grade oral mucositis is 48%1—pausing cabozantinib is unwarranted as the minimally symptomatic lesions do not align with the typical presentation of oral mucositis, characterized by painful ulcerations and fibrinous exudate, favoring nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces (choice B).2The absence of a cheesy white exudate that can be scraped off, with an underlying red patch, makes oral candidiasis unlikely (choice C). Geographic tongue is an inflammatory condition of unclear etiology, characterized by erythematous, multifocal, patches circumscribed by white, elevated, hyperkeratotic margins along the dorsolateral aspect of the tongue.3,4These lesions result from the loss of filiform papillae, often coalesce, and exhibit intermittent relapsing and remitting patterns with exacerbations ranging from days to years.3,4Recurrent lesions often affect new areas, producing dynamic migratory patterns as epithelial proliferation and exfoliation at different sites create a maplike appearance. While most cases are asymptomatic, up to 25% of patients report a burning sensation (or irritation, soreness, or pain) over atrophic patches, typically triggered by hot, spicy, or acidic foods.3,5The diagnosis is primarily clinical. The prevalence of geographic tongue in the general population is estimated to be between 1.0% to 2.5%.3,4The condition is most frequently seen in children and young adults, decreases in frequency with age, and may have a female predominance.6Increased prevalence with family history and associations with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles suggest a possible genetic component.7Geographic tongue has been associated with various conditions, including psoriasis, juvenile diabetes, allergies, anemia, endocrinopathies, Down syndrome, and reactive arthritis. Geographic tongue may represent an oral manifestation of psoriasis, given the reported presence in up to 14% of individuals with psoriasis, the frequent psoriasiform histologic features, and the presence of shared HLA-Cw6 marker.7Differential diagnoses, such as leukoplakia, lichen planus, candidiasis, and herpes simplex virus, can usually be ruled out based on history (lack of migratory patterns), examination, and histopathologic findings if needed. A biopsy is indicated only if the diagnosis is in doubt. Histologically, geographic tongue resembles psoriasis. The white, elevated areas of the lesions exhibit a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate at times undergoing exocytosis with subsequent microabscess and pustule formation as well as acanthosis and parakeratosis. The smooth, erythematous regions contain a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate with vascular ectasia and loss of filiform papillae, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy. Geographic tongue has been reported alongside the use of angiogenesis inhibitors, including anti–vascular endothelial growth factor agents and receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, and sunitinib.8Prior case series have reported geographic tongue occurring on average 6 months after bevacizumab initiation, primarily in female individualss.9The temporal association here—a first and hitherto only episode of geographic tongue occurring 3 months after initiating cabozantinib— makes cabozantinib a plausible etiology of geographic tongue in this case. Drug-associated geographic tongue does not have known oncologic ramifications, does not typically require drug modification or discontinuation, and does not typically require specific treatment.8 Reassurance is critical for patients given the dramatic appearance of the lesions, especially in the context of cancer and cancer treatment. Topical analgesics such as lidocaine can be offered to manage burning/pain, alongside avoiding triggering foods. No specific treatments are typically indicated, although tacrolimus swish-and-spit treatment has shown promising data in patients with resistant disease.3Antihistamines, gabapentinoids, topical corticosteroids, and antifungals lack consistent evidence.3 The patient was counseled and reassured regarding the condition, no changes to cabozantinib were made, and no specific treatment was initiated. The lesions spontaneously resolved after 2 weeks. The patient continued cabozantinib. No recurrent lesions were noted at last follow-up 5 months later.

caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
scenario: A 50-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with a 10-year history of recurrent plaque outbreaks between her toes. She had a history of Bowen disease in the anus that had been treated with excision and skin grafting. Physical examination revealed multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes and on the vulva (Figure 1). Additionally, a 5 × 4 × 1-cm ulcerated perianal tumor with easy bleeding was noted. Coagulation, thyroid, liver, and kidney test results were within the normal ranges. Tests for syphilis, HIV, and autoantibodies were negative. However, the foot lesions were positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) 16, and the perianal, vulvar, and cervical lesions were positive for HPV-6, HPV-16, and HPV-18. A complete blood cell count revealed a decreased lymphocyte count of 400/μL (range, 1100-3200/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The T-cell subset panel showed a total lymphocyte count of 564.45 cells/mL (range, 1200-3400 cells/mL) and a CD4+T-cell count of 59.95 cells/mL (range, 410-884 cells/mL).

options.B: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma

answer: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma
explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

caption: A, Clinical photograph showing a 70-year-old man with generalized muscle wasting except for bilateral hypertrophy of shoulder muscles, also known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. B, Deltoid muscle biopsy showing deposition of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels (black arrowhead) and between muscle fibers (pink arrowhead) (hematoxylin-eosin stain, original magnification ×1000).
scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of hypertension and chronic migraine presented with 10 months’ history of progressive generalized muscle weakness and stiffness. He reported a 19-kg unintentional weight loss over the last 7 months. He described worsening exertional dyspnea over the past 3 weeks prior to presentation. He had multiple surgical procedures for joint contractures and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in the past 5 years. He had no history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Physical examination revealed generalized muscle wasting except for hypertrophy of bilateral shoulder muscles (Figure 1A) with proximal muscle weakness of the shoulders. The reflexes and sensation were intact in both upper limbs, and there was no distal weakness. Initial workup showed a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), serum creatinine level of 1.9 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4; normal range, 0.7-1.3 mg/dL), serum albumin level of 3.4 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10; normal range, 3.4-5.4 g/dL), and serum calcium level of 10.2 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.25; normal range, 8.5-10.2 mg/dL). Creatine kinase level was 843 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167; normal range, 22-198 U/L). Urinalysis showed isolated proteinuria without cellular casts, and subsequent 24-hour urine collection revealed 1.7 g of protein. Magnetic resonance imaging of the shoulders showed decreased T1 signal intensity of the bone marrow and increased T2 signal intensity of the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups, with minimal signal intensity alteration of the muscles. A deltoid muscle biopsy with hematoxylin-eosin staining revealed deposition of amorphous material (Figure 1B).
explanation: This patient presented with pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles (Figure 1A). The light microscopic examination of the deltoid muscle biopsy revealed deposits of pink, amorphous material within the walls of blood vessels and between muscle fibers (Figure 1B). The deposits had positive results on Congo red staining and demonstrated yellow-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy (Figure 2). A bone marrow biopsy showed 70% involvement by IgG λ light chain (AL) restricted plasma cells. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of immunoglobulin AL amyloid myopathy with multiple myeloma was made. Amyloid myopathy is rare. Among 3434 patients with AL amyloidosis seen at the Mayo Clinic between 1995 and 2015, only 1.5% had a diagnosis of amyloid myopathy confirmed by muscle biopsy.1Although amyloid myopathy is typically associated with systemic amyloidosis, it can occur in isolation—affecting only the muscles—in about one-quarter of cases, which complicates the diagnosis further.2Furthermore, amyloid myopathy is an underdiagnosed condition, often identified late in the disease course, with a median time from the onset of symptoms to diagnosis of 23 months.1,3 Similar to this patient’s findings, most patients with amyloid myopathy report proximal muscle weakness. Other common manifestations include myalgia, muscle atrophy, muscle claudication, contracture with reduced mobility, and macroglossia.1Soft tissue amyloid deposition leading to pseudohypertrophy of the shoulder muscles creates the distinctive appearance known as the Hercules look and the shoulder pad sign. In this patient, the combination of weight loss, proteinuria, elevated serum creatinine and creatine kinase levels, and magnetic resonance imaging findings—characterized by increased T2 signal intensity in the subcutaneous fat between muscle groups (atypical for inflammatory myopathy)—suggested an unusual etiology for the proximal muscle weakness and triggered muscle biopsy. There is no established diagnostic consensus specifically for amyloid myopathy. Instead, the diagnostic approach typically aligns with the criteria for AL amyloidosis as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group, requiring the presence of all the following 4 criteria: (1) presence of an amyloid-related systemic syndrome, (2) positive results on amyloid staining by Congo red in tissue, (3) evidence that amyloid is related to light chain either by direct examination using mass spectrometry proteomic analysis or immunoelectron microscopy, and (4) evidence of a monoclonal plasma cell disorder.4 All patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis should undergo evaluation to assess their eligibility for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (ASCT).5Studies have shown that ASCT is both safe and effective in carefully selected patients, including those 70 years and older.6Induction chemotherapy for AL amyloidosis typically relies on regimens adapted from those used in multiple myeloma. However, the presence of amyloid-related dysfunction in 1 or more organs significantly impacts survival and can restrict a patient’s ability to tolerate aggressive treatments.7 This patient was found to have cardiac involvement by amyloidosis. He initially underwent induction chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone followed by ASCT, achieving a very good partial response. However, 17 months later, he experienced a biochemical relapse. One month later, he was hospitalized with pneumonia and septic shock and died during that admission. Amyloid myopathy can be a presenting feature of AL amyloidosis, with or without multiple myeloma. Timely diagnosis is crucial, as it is often underrecognized, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment.

caption: A,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) showing FDG uptake in the perirenal space (white arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions with FDG uptake (yellow arrowheads). B, Abdomen CT showing perirenal fibrosis (arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions in the sacrum.
scenario: A 72-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera (positive forJAK2V617F) presented with several months of functional decline and weight loss. Previous imaging obtained a year prior showed hepatomegaly (18 cm) and mild perinephric stranding bilaterally. On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Initial workup showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 11.8 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 106 μm3), thrombocytopenia (88 × 103/μL), normal white blood cell count (5.19 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) with lymphopenia (0.72 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]), elevated alkaline phosphatase (655 U/L; reference, 41-133 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]), and hyperbilirubinemia (total, 2.1 mg/dL; reference, 0.3-1.2; direct, 1.3 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104]) with otherwise normal levels of creatinine, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

options.A: POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, skin changes) syndrome

distractors: POEMS (polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal plasma cell disorder, skin changes) syndrome
explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

caption: A, Endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) grade 2, with solid and microacinar type growth seen toward the top left of the image (hematoxylin-eosin stain; original magnification ×10). B, Wild-type expression of p53 is seen in the top right of the image, but the majority of the tumor showed an aberrant null pattern of p53 immunohistochemistry expression (p53 immunohistochemistry; original magnification ×20).
scenario: A 65-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Endometrial biopsy showed International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) grade 2 endometrioid adenocarcinoma (Figure, A). She underwent a total laparoscopic hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and sentinel lymph node biopsy. Pathological assessment revealed FIGO grade 2 endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma invading into the outer half of the myometrium, without evident lymphovascular invasion. The cervix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes were unremarkable, and the lymph nodes were not involved. Immunohistochemically, the tumor showed intact nuclear expression of the mismatch repair (MMR) proteins and a distinctive subclonal null pattern of p53 expression (Figure, B). Next-generation sequencing identified a pathogenicPOLEmutation (c.857C>G).

options.A: Determine this endometrial cancer is of POLE-mutated subtype.
options.B: Determine this endometrial cancer is of MMR-deficient subtype.
options.C: Determine this endometrial cancer is of no specific molecular profile subtype.
options.D: Determine this endometrial cancer is of p53 abnormal subtype.

answer: Determine this endometrial cancer is ofPOLE-mutated subtype.
distractors: Determine this endometrial cancer is of MMR-deficient subtype.
Determine this endometrial cancer is of no specific molecular profile subtype.
Determine this endometrial cancer is of p53 abnormal subtype.
explanation: A. Determine this endometrial cancer is ofPOLE-mutated subtype. In 2013, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project identified 4 molecular subtypes of endometrial cancer, each with distinct clinical outcomes.1Groupings closely approximating the original TGCA subtypes can be pragmatically identified using immunohistochemistry (IHC) for MMR and p53, and next-generation sequencing for evaluation ofPOLE. The World Health Organization and FIGO 2023 staging system have endorsed this classifier, and the 4 subtypes are referred to asPOLEmutated, MMR deficient, p53 abnormal, and no specific molecular profile.2,3﻿POLE-mutated tumors (5%-10% of all endometrial cancers) are defined by the presence of pathogenicPOLEmutations, of which 11 have been currently established (Box).4These occur in the exonuclease domain and have been proven to generate the characteristic ultramutated phenotype of this subgroup and confer a favorable outcome, in part because of the known robust intratumoral T-cell response caused by an enrichment of antigenic neopeptides.5Although these neoplasms do demonstrate some relatively characteristic histological changes (often high grade in appearance and with subclonal or diffuse MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities indicative of secondary/resultant mutations), they cannot be reliably identified by pathological examination alone,6and Sanger or next-generation sequencing of thePOLEexonuclease domain is required for this purpose. Molecular classification of endometrial cancer is widely accepted as the standard of care in the diagnosis and management of this disease, and knowledge ofPOLEmutation status is critically important because the presence of a pathogenic mutation is thought to modify the importance of certain histopathologic and immunohistochemical findings (eg, histotype/tumor grade, abnormal expression patterns of p53). This case is an example of a tumor with underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation as well as subclonal abnormal p53 immunoexpression. When more than 1 classifying feature is seen in a tumor, the neoplasm is known as a multiple classifier. Approximately 3% to 11% of all endometrial cancers are multiple classifiers. A previous study revealed that tumors with pathogenicPOLEmutations in addition to MMR and/or p53 IHC abnormalities mostly cluster with single classifierPOLE-mutated tumors when evaluated by hierarchical clustering of TCGA endometrial cancers, based on single nucleotide variant type and somatic copy number alterations.7In addition, evidence to date suggests that multiple classifierPOLE-driven tumors also exhibit favorable clinical behavior.7-9As such, any tumor harboring a pathogenicPOLEmutation—regardless of abnormalities with MMR or p53 IHC staining, which in isolation may predict more aggressive behavior—should be classified asPOLEmutated.7 Because of the identification of an underlying pathogenicPOLEmutation in the tumor, this patient was offered and consented to participation in the international EN10/RAINBO (Refining Adjuvant Treatment in Endometrial Cancer Based on Molecular Features) BLUE trial evaluating de-escalation of adjuvant treatment inPOLE-mutated endometrial cancer.

caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
scenario: A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 weeks of recurrent fevers (temperature up to 39.5 °C), malaise, night sweats, 30-lb unintentional weight loss, and dyspnea. The patient had a COVID-19 infection 2 months before presentation. Rheumatologic and infectious workup was unrevealing, including negative HIV and hepatitis test results. Imaging was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and a likely liver hemangioma measuring 3 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm. Hospital admission laboratory values showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10) with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Fasting triglycerides level was elevated to 404 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113) and ferritin level was elevated to 1357.7 ng/dL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1). Fibrinogen was normal at 429 mg/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 0.01) and lactate dehydrogenase was minimally elevated to 291 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Liver function test results were normal. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for a hematologic malignancy but showed scant hemophagocytes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan demonstrated splenomegaly with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.4 (Figure 1). The spleen measured 19.5 cm on ultrasonography. Soluble CD25 level was elevated to 7657.3 pg/mL. The patient met 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria. Liver biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytes only. The patient started taking empirical dexamethasone, 10 mg/m2, for possible hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with resolution of fevers. Weeks later, while tapering corticosteroids, the patient deteriorated with hypotension, persistent fevers, and hypoxemia. Repeat PET-CT showed worsening splenomegaly (maximum standardized uptake value, 5.7). The patient was readmitted for further evaluation.

options.D: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

caption: A 6-cm heterogeneous cauliflower-shaped exophytic tumor at the anal margin.
scenario: A 27-year-old male patient without any known medical history presented with anal discomfort and pruritus for 3 months. He did not report any abdominal pain or transit disorder and denied smoking, alcohol consumption, or any recent travel. Physical examination revealed a 6-cm heterogeneous cauliflower-shaped exophytic tumor at the anal margin with no extension to the scrotum or the rectum (Figure 1). No inguinal lymph nodes were detected and the examination of the integuments revealed no other visible lesion. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. The digital rectal examination was normal and revealed no rectal bleeding. Hemoglobin, white blood cell count, platelet count, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, gamma glutamyl transferase, total, direct and indirect bilirubin, serum albumin, and calcium values were all within the normal limits. Serology results for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis were negative. After thorough investigation, the patient did not present any deterioration in general condition and had no known family history of malignant and gastrointestinal diseases.

options.D: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal

distractors: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal
explanation: Multiple biopsies of the anal lesion yielded a diagnosis of p16-positive condyloma. A surgical excision was performed. However, the analysis of the surgical specimen identified a giant condyloma acuminatum (Figure 2), known as Buschke-Löwenstein tumor (BLT), with foci transformed into squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) extending to the resection margins (R1 resection). Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan revealed no suspicious lymph nodes or distant metastases. Giant condyloma acuminatum, or BLT, is a rare sexually transmitted disease of the anogenital region that occurs preferentially in males in their 40s, with an estimated incidence less than 0.1% in the general population.1Although considered benign, BLT is characterized by its local aggressive potential, a high recurrence rate after treatment, and a possible transformation into SCC.1Typical BLT presents as a slow-growing cauliflowerlike mass that may initially be mistaken for a common condyloma. It can also develop rapidly, especially in immunocompromised patients who are at increased risk of the disease.2As a consequence, sexual transmitted diseases such as HIV, hepatitis B and C, and syphilis must be systematically ruled out. BLT pathogenesis involves low-risk human papillomaviruses (HPVs) such as HPV-6 and HPV-11, but the mechanisms underlying the progression from low-risk HPV-driven condyloma acuminatum to BLT remain largely unknown.3The diagnosis is based on its histological presentation characterized by hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, acanthosis, and koilocytosis.4Neoplastic transformation is frequent and features of SCC, carcinoma in situ, and verrucous carcinoma must be sought.5 Given the lack of consensus and the paucity of available studies, the treatment of BLT is challenging. Radical surgery, ranging from wide excision to abdominoperineal amputation, is the most frequently offered treatment.6However, a number of therapeutic approaches have been proposed, including radiotherapy, chemotherapy, electrocoagulation, and cryotherapy. Recently, Costa Almeida et al7developed a therapeutic algorithm based on a review of clinical cases in which R0 resection was the first-line treatment. This algorithm suggests that neoadjuvant radiochemotherapy should be discussed to increase the chances of complete resection, adjuvant radiotherapy should be proposed in the event of transformation to SCC, and exclusive radiochemotherapy should be considered in patients ineligible for surgery. Morbidity is related both to the tumor and to the treatment, which can result in severe soft tissue infections, necrosis, fistulas, flap failure, anal stenosis. or incontinence. Additionally, morbidity and mortality are associated with recurrences, which occur in approximately 50% of patients, and histological malignant transformation.8 In the present case, therapeutic options were discussed by a multidisciplinary tumor board. Because of the microinfiltration of SCC within the surgical specimen and the R1 resection, adjuvant anopelvic radiotherapy with concurrent capecitabine was proposed. Radiochemotherapy was well tolerated. Three months after the treatment, the patient showed no evidence of recurrence or treatment-related adverse effects. He remains under close medical supervision. This case illustrates the importance of knowing this rare tumor with significant local aggressiveness, a high risk of recurrence and malignant transformation, which can be mistaken for a common condyloma at first.
