Neuroretinitis may be infectious, noninfectious, or idiopathic.B henselae, which causes cat-scratch disease, is the most common infectious culprit, but numerous other pathogens, including syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, and toxoplasmosis, can also cause neuroretinitis.2,3A thorough history, for example eliciting evidence of a prodromal illness after contact with kittens (cat-scratch disease) or travel to tuberculosis-endemic regions, may guide serologic evaluation. Noninfectious causes of neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, polyarteritis nodosa, idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis and an idiopathic form (diagnosis of exclusion) that may recur.2 Neuroretinitis is a diagnosis based on clinical features, classically including optic nerve head edema and macular exudates in a stellate distribution (ie, macular star). However, the appearance of a macular star may be delayed 2 weeks or more after symptom onset, so a star may not be evident if the patient is examined early in the disease course.3Macular stars are not specific for neuroretinitis, but instead form due to the exudative macular detachment secondary to optic disc edema. This association has also been described in papilledema, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy, and diabetic papillopathy.2,4In this case, a macular star developed 5 weeks after symptom onset. Management ofB henselaeneuroretinitis is controversial but may include systemic antibiotics and corticosteroids,5especially in cases of severe vision loss. This patient was treated with the standard regimen of doxycycline and rifampin,6and because his vision began to improve, steroids were deferred. In collaboration with pediatric infectious disease specialists, results of investigations for systemic manifestations of bartonellosis, including fever, hepatosplenomegaly, osteomyelitis, and endocarditis, were negative. No consensus guidelines exist to guide long-term management, so the dual antibiotic regimen was continued until subretinal fluid resolved approximately 2 months after initial presentation; antibiotics were discontinued shortly thereafter. At 2 months, mild compromise of outer retinal structures was evident by optical coherence tomography. Over the following months, serial imaging revealed partial reconstitution of foveal photoreceptor outer segment integrity (Figure 2) and continued improvement in visual acuity, which was 20/60 at last follow-up 8 months after presentation.

caption: A, Fundus photographs of the left eye and the right eye (inset) showed optic disc pallor with blurred disc margins. The left eye had discontiguous blood flow in the superior retinal vessels (arrowheads). B, Fundus fluorescein angiography of the left eye showed microaneurysms at both the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina.
scenario: A 14-year old girl presented with sudden painless vision decline in the left eye for 5 days, without vision decline in the right eye. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU 6 months earlier. She reported constant fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in the lower limbs, and intermittent claudication over the past 12 months, with no history of trauma, surgery, COVID-19 infection, influenza, or other infection. Visual acuity was light perception OD and no light perception OS. Both pupils dilated, with the right eye reacting sluggishly to light and the left eye being nonreactive. Intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Posterior examination revealed optic disc edema in each eye, and the left eye had a swollen and pale optic disc with segmental blood flow in retinal vessels (Figure 1A). Fluorescein angiography of the left eye had prolonged arm-to-retina circulation time and multiple microaneurysms at the superotemporal and inferotemporal retina (Figure 1B). Visual evoked potentials were negative in both eyes. She had an increased white blood cell count (10 540/μL; to convert to ×109per liter, multiply by 0.001) and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (73 mm/h) and had positive findings for cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody and antinuclear antibody. Other serology test results were negative, including hepatitis B and C virus, HIV, rapid plasma reagin, and anti–double-stranded DNA.

options.A: Perform diagnostic anterior chamber and/or vitreous tap

distractors: Perform diagnostic anterior chamber and/or vitreous tap
explanation: C. Obtain brain magnetic resonance imaging For bilateral optic edema, ocular infection should be considered. The most clinically relevant slitlamp findings of the patient were optic disc edema in both eyes and abnormal pupil reaction to the light with no sign of infection. Her blood test results did not suggest systemic infection; therefore, a diagnostic intravitreal tap (choice A) would not be a preferred next step. Providing intravitreal corticosteroids (choice B) would not address the systemic symptoms, and no obvious retinal vascular inflammatory abnormalities were noted on fluorescein angiography. The patient had no family history of inherited genetic disorders to warrant genetic testing (choice D). The patient reported fatigue, occasional dizziness and headache, mild pain in her lower limbs, and intermittent claudication and had findings of elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, and antinuclear antibody, suggesting the need for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (choice C). Brain MRI showed an abnormally high signal intensity in the left periventricular white matter (Figure 2) and was suspicious for a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Since MRI showed features consistent with a demyelinating disorder or local cerebral infarction in the left periventricular white matter, suggesting a systemic disease rather than optic neuritis, urgent referral to rheumatology was recommended for further investigation of systemic autoimmune diseases. The rheumatologist suspected Takayasu arteritis and arranged magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and arterial angiography for the head and neck. Both MRA and arterial angiography showed left common carotid artery and internal carotid artery occlusion, with right innominate artery and right common carotid artery stenosis, distal arterial occlusion, and multiple collateral arteries to the brain parenchyma (Figure 2), confirming a diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Subsequently, 400 mg of prednisone was given intravenously for 3 days. After 1 day, visual acuity improved to 20/32 OD and remained substantially impaired at hand motions OS, without further improvement. Takayasu arteritis is a rare autoimmune disease associated with inflammation of large vessels, such as the aorta and its main branches. It is known as pulseless disease and occurs commonly in young Asian women younger than 40 years.1Diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis may be challenging with lack of specific clinical symptoms and sensitive laboratory tests.2It is usually asymptomatic in the early stage, gradually proceeding to ischemic complications. Chronic ischemia can be associated with various clinical presentations, depending on the pattern of arterial involvement.3,4 Only approximately 9.6% cases present with vision loss as an initial clinical feature.5A comprehensive medical history and detailed physical examinations could provide valuable information to direct subsequent investigations. Diagnostic criteria for Takayasu arteritis consist of findings from imaging, laboratory tests, and physical examinations, eg, subclavian artery lesion, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and carotid artery tenderness.6On diagnosis, prompt and aggressive treatment using glucocorticoid therapy along with conventional immunosuppressive agents should be initiated, and surgical revascularization may be considered.7,8Long-term follow-up is recommended, especially for younger patients, due to a high relapse rate.9 After approximately 4 weeks of treatment, the patient’s dosage of glucocorticoid had been reduced to daily oral methylprednisolone acetate, 20 mg, along with oral methotrexate, 10 mg once per week. Her visual acuity remains 20/32 OD and counting fingers OS, and her physical symptoms have resolved.

caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
scenario: A Hispanic woman in her 40s was referred for an asymptomatic epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Ocular history included amblyopia of the left eye. Medical history included chronic neuropathy, ataxia, and myelopathy of unknown etiology for which she was followed up by a neurologist. Family history was positive for consanguinity, but there were no known inherited conditions. Genetic testing showed a homozygous variant of undetermined significance in theSACSgene and a variant of undetermined significance in theSLC5A7gene, but it was inconclusive whether these variants were related to her systemic conditions. Review of systems was otherwise negative. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Fundus examination revealed prominent peripapillary retinal nerve fibers with papillomacular bundle fine striae and slightly blunted foveal light reflex. There was also an irregular sheen of the nasal macula in both eyes, greater in the left eye (Figure 1). Axial length was 22.93 mm in the right eye and 22.10 mm in the left eye, with anterior chamber depth of 3.44 mm and 3.37 mm in the right and left eye, respectively.

options.B: Obtain optical coherence tomography of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer
options.C: Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling

answer: Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)
distractors: Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling
explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

caption: External photograph of right upper eyelid lesions. Examination of the patient’s right upper eyelid on presentation demonstrated a central lesion with thickening of the margin and an ulcerated and erythematous nodule near the medial canthus.
scenario: A 75-year-old woman presented with a history of enlarging, erythematous right upper eyelid lesions. She reported approximately 3 months of symptoms, with initial development of a single erythematous lesion along the eyelid margin. The lesion had previously been evaluated by another practitioner who diagnosed a hordeolum and prescribed erythromycin ointment and warm compresses. However, the lesion became progressively larger with development of a second medial lesion over the ensuing 2 months, prompting referral. She denied pain, trauma, and prior skin cancer. Her medical history was notable for essential thrombocythemia (ET) with calreticulin (CALR) gene variation. Her ocular history was notable for an upper eyelid blepharoplasty 20 years prior but was otherwise unremarkable. Examination of the right upper eyelid demonstrated a central lesion with a thickened eyelid margin, madarosis, and inspissated glands, and a medial nodular and erythematous lesion with overlying ulceration (Figure 1). There was minimal tenderness to palpation. There was no proptosis, and her extraocular muscle movements were full. There was mild conjunctival injection of the right eye without any conjunctival lesions. The remainder of her ocular examination was unremarkable.
explanation: ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma B. Biopsy of eyelid lesions Despite initial treatment for suspected hordeolum, the patient’s eyelid lesions progressively enlarged with new madarosis and ulceration. This raised concern for malignancy including sebaceous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, and squamous cell carcinoma, prompting biopsy (option B) as the next step. Intralesional corticosteroid injection for acute chalazion (option A), oral antibiotics for preseptal cellulitis (option C), and oral corticosteroids for inflammatory disease (option D) were not indicated given the clinical presentation and concern for malignancy. Histopathology demonstrated medium cells with horseshoe nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and mitotic figures that were CD30+, Ki67+, and ALK−, consistent with ALK− anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) (Figure 2). Initial systemic imaging showed no systemic involvement, leading to a diagnosis of primary cutaneous ALCL. Primary cutaneous ALCL is a CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorder that may present as rapidly growing localized lesions in the face, trunk, or extremities.1It may be classified as ALK+ and ALK− based on presence of ALK-fusion proteins, with ALK− ALCL typically having worse prognosis due to delayed diagnosis or poor response to treatment.2,3Treatment options include CHOP chemotherapy (ie, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone), radiotherapy, or surgical resection.1 Eyelid lymphoma is overall rare, composing 5% of ocular adnexal lymphomas, and tends to be of B-cell origin.4,5ALCL involving the eyelid is very uncommon, with fewer than 25 reported cases.5,6Its infrequent presentation often leads to misdiagnosis as other periorbital pathology, such as chalazion or squamous cell carcinoma, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment.6Concerning features of progression despite treatment, development of new lesions, madarosis, or ulceration warrant biopsy. The patient’s history of ET, a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm, may have increased the risk of ALCL. ET is associated with increased risk of secondary hematological malignancies and solid tumors.7ALK− ALCL associated with ET is rare, with only 1 prior report of central nervous system ALK− ALCL occurring in a patient with ET without skin or eyelid involvement.8ET may potentially increase the risk of developing ALCL due to abnormalities of the JAK-STAT pathway.9This patient had a variant in theCALRgene, which is involved in this pathway and may deregulate hematopoietic stem cell clonal expansion while disrupting natural immunosurveillance.9Physicians should consider malignancy in persistent or enlarging eyelid lesions, especially in patients with hematological conditions such as ET. Prompt biopsy may lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment, potentially improving prognosis in patients with ALK− ALCL. In subsequent oncology visits, the patient developed new skin lesions along her face and body, with repeat biopsy confirming the same ALK− ALCL. She received orbital radiation for her eyelid lesions and started weekly methotrexate, with resolution of her eyelid lesions and marginal improvement of her other lesions. However, further testing revealed central nervous system involvement, suggesting systemic ALCL for which she began systemic and intrathecal chemotherapy. Her eyelid lesions represented the first manifestation of systemic disease, highlighting the importance of vigilance and a high index of suspicion as well as prompt biopsy to facilitate timely diagnosis and treatment.

caption: A, Fundus photograph of the right eye showing an infratemporal exudative retinal detachment. Inset, Choroidal folds in the macula. B, B-scan ultrasonography demonstrating broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve in addition to the presence of a retinal detachment. C, T1 axial orbital magnetic resonance image (MRI) with gadolinium showing the right eye retinal detachment and revealing an enhancing right optic nerve mass.
scenario: A 63-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes presented with gradually progressive vision loss in the right eye for the past year. Her visual acuity on presentation was 20/80 OD and 20/25 OS. Anterior examination findings of both eyes were normal with clear posterior chamber intraocular lenses. Fundus examination of the right eye showed choroidal folds and a macula-involving retinal detachment with no identifiable retinal break and shifting subretinal fluid (Figure 1A). Fundus examination findings in the left eye were normal. Fluorescein angiography did not identify areas of leakage. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated broad areas of low reflectivity within the sub-Tenon space and around the optic nerve (Figure 1B). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a contrast-enhancing area of soft-tissue thickening encircling the right optic nerve (Figure 1C). Serologies for syphilis, Lyme disease, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis were negative. Chest radiographic findings were unremarkable.

options.C: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair
options.D: Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion

answer: Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion
distractors: Perform pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair
explanation: Low-grade B-cell lymphoma associated with exudative retinal detachment D. Perform biopsy of the optic nerve lesion This case represents orbital lymphoma masquerading as posterior scleritis, both of which may cause choroidal folds, exudative retinal detachments, and sub-Tenon fluid. Given the lack of retinal break, vitrectomy for repair of the retinal detachment would not have addressed the underlying etiology (answer C). B-scan ultrasonography in this patient’s case revealed a focus of low reflectivity adjacent to the optic nerve (Figure 1B), which was felt to be atypical of posterior scleritis and prompted orbital MRI that showed soft-tissue thickening around the optic nerve (Figure 1C). After negative results on infectious and inflammatory workup, differential diagnosis included idiopathic orbital inflammation (IOI), lymphoma, or other lymphoproliferative processes. Whereas IOI typically presents acutely and with pain, the course of this patient’s vision loss was insidious and nonpainful. Moreover, IOI is a diagnosis of exclusion. Empirical treatment for IOI with oral prednisone could reduce biopsy yield in the case of lymphoma or lymphoproliferative processes (answer A). Given the potentially life-threatening nature of orbital lymphoma, observation with interval orbital MRI would not be appropriate (answer B). Positron emission tomography did not reveal extraorbital lesions amenable to biopsy. Consequently, orbital biopsy was performed via transconjunctival incision with takedown of the medial rectus muscle (answer D). Prior to surgery, extensive discussion with the patient covered procedural risks, including severe vision loss. The orbital biopsy specimen underwent histologic correlation and flow cytometry, which identified low-grade B-cell lymphoma. Although rare, orbital lymphomas are the most common type of orbital malignant neoplasm, usually presenting as a low-grade B-cell lymphoma or extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type.1Classically, it presents as an insidiously progressive and painless orbital process in middle-aged and older individuals.2While early diagnosis of orbital lymphoma is critical for the preservation of vision, delay of diagnosis can occur due to nonspecific orbital symptoms among orbital inflammatory and neoplastic processes.3Despite advances in using conventional MRI features and imaging-related values to differentiate orbital lymphoma from orbital inflammatory processes,4currently, adequate imaging studies followed by early surgical biopsy are key for achieving early diagnosis.5 On diagnostic confirmation by the pathologist, patients should be sent to the oncologist and/or radiation oncologist for consultation. Excellent local control may be achieved for low-grade lymphomas with a conventional radiotherapy dose ranging from 24 to 40 Gy. Alternatively, recent studies suggest that a low-dose course (defined as 2 Gy × 2 fractions) with salvage therapy in the case of locoregional relapse may achieve comparable outcomes, although further multicenter studies are warranted.6,7 This patient underwent low-dose radiotherapy treatment to the right orbit, which led to reduction of the optic nerve mass and resolution of the retinal detachment (Figure 2). This was associated with improvement in visual acuity to 20/25 OD. This case demonstrates the vital role imaging plays in ruling out tumors as a cause for exudative retinal detachment masquerading as posterior scleritis.

caption: Red-free scanning laser ophthalmoscopy images revealing extensive retinal vascular sheathing (inset: macular edema seen on optical coherence tomography; fluorescein angiogram revealed late dye leakage).
scenario: A previously healthy 20-year-old Asian woman was hospitalized in the neurology department after experiencing fever, malaise, headache, nausea, vomiting, and neck stiffness for 2 weeks. Computed tomography scan results revealed meningoencephalitis. Her systemic inflammatory markers were elevated, including a left-shifted leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 19 610 μL (normal values, 3500-9500 μL), a monocyte count of 900 × 103μL (normal values, 100-600 × 103μL), and normal C-reactive protein level. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were suggestive of viral meningoencephalitis, including elevated protein levels (0.074 g/dL; normal values, 0.015-0.045 g/dL) and increased leucocyte (93 × 106/L; normal values, 0-8 × 106/L). Cytological examination showed an increase in lymphocytes. Intracranial pressure was elevated (>320 mm H2O), and the glucose level was 2.08 mmol/L (normal values, 2.5-4.5 mmol/L). On day 2 of hospitalization, the patient experienced blurred vision in both eyes. Her visual acuity was 20/500 in both eyes. Both eyes had normal pupillary responses, color vision, and intraocular pressures. The results of an anterior chamber examination were unremarkable. The results of scanning laser ophthalmoscopy of both eyes revealed substantial inflammation, including marked disc edema, retinal vein dilation and tortuosity, extensive retinal vascular sheathing (Figure 1). Optical coherence tomography showed vitritis and cystoid macular edema in both eyes. Fluorescein angiogram revealed tortuous dilatation of retinal venous vessels with fluorescence leakage, while the optic disc exhibited hyperfluorescence.

options.C: Initiate immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin
options.D: Intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor

distractors: Initiate immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin
Intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor
explanation: B. Evaluate for systemic infectious disease Administering systemic corticosteroids (choice A) would not be the preferred answer because corticosteroids could suppress the immune response, potentially worsening an undiagnosed infectious process. Initiating immunomodulatory therapy with intravenous immunoglobulin (choice C) was not recommended as the next step because intravenous immunoglobulin is typically used for autoimmune or inflammatory conditions rather than primary infectious diseases. Performing an intravitreal injection with anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (choice D) would not be the next recommended step because there was not proof that the cystoid macular edema was vascular endothelial growth factor driven vs inflammation driven. This patient was diagnosed with bilateral frosted branch angiitis (FBA). FBA may be idiopathic or associated with infections, inflammation, or tumors.1Prior to initiating intraocular or systemic corticosteroid treatment, it is important to exclude infectious diseases. Bacterial cultures of the patient’s cerebrospinal fluid were negative. However, next-generation sequencing of the cerebrospinal fluid indicated Epstein-Barr virus infection. Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with FBA combined with viral meningoencephalitis and treated with ganciclovir and corticosteroids. The termfrosted branch angiitiswas first reported by Ito et al2in 1976 and named after its distinctive retinal appearance. FBA is a rare retinal vasculitis characterized by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration of the perivascular space.1,2The co-occurrence of viral meningoencephalitis and FBA is uncommon. FBA predominantly affects young, healthy individuals, with a higher prevalence in female individuals (61%) compared with male individuals (39%). The age at onset has a bimodal distribution, peaking in childhood and between ages 25 and 30 years. Favorable prognoses have been observed in patients undergoing systemic corticosteroid therapy.3Common conditions associated with FBA include cytomegalovirus retinitis, HIV retinitis, and toxoplasma chorioretinitis.4,5However, several systemic diseases may be associated with FBA, including graft vs host disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, Crohn disease, large cell lymphoma, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.6-8The prognosis of FBA is variable,9and may be complicated by macular scarring, retinal neovascularization, or epiretinal membranes. Clinicians, including infectious disease specialists and ophthalmologists, should be aware of the vision-threatening potential of FBA and try to provide timely diagnosis and treatment, potentially reducing the risk of poor ocular outcomes. Patients with FBA may experience a sudden decrease in visual acuity. Severe cases may result in light perception, although some patients maintain 20/20 visual acuity in both eyes.1Fluorescein angiogram may be important to diagnosis FBA, as it can reveal extensive perivascular fluorescein leakage. High-dose corticosteroids have been associated with resolution of retinal abnormalities and improvement of visual acuity in idiopathic FBA. Cases associated with systemic disease typically will need treatment of the primary disease along with corticosteroids for the retina. Some patients may experience relapse if the primary disease recurs.4The extensive vasculitis and sensitivity to short-term corticosteroid treatment suggest that FBA might be a specific vascular reaction triggered by various stimuli, potentially mediated by immune complexes.10 The patient received high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy and ganciclovir. Four weeks later, the FBA and macular edema had disappeared (Figure 2). Seven weeks later, the patient’s visual acuity improved to 20/40 in both eyes. Continued vision loss is likely due to delayed functional recovery compared with structural recovery.

caption: Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluoresence imaging in the left (A) and right (B) eyes.
scenario: A 46-year-old woman was referred for a second opinion regarding hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), diabetes type 1, nonalcoholic steatohepatosis, mild congenital hearing loss, and anemia. SLE was managed with azathioprine and belimumab, and she had been taking hydroxychloroquine, 400 mg, daily for 5 years before the medication was recently stopped due to concern for retinal toxicity. Review of systems was notable for imbalance, cognitive decline, major depression, and recent onset of suspected seizures. Snellen visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/20 OS and intraocular pressures were normal. Results of slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable, with clear corneas, quiet anterior chambers, and clear lenses bilaterally. Fundus examination revealed bilateral discrete perifoveal circular areas of atrophy. The optic discs and fundus were otherwise unremarkable. Fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed perifoveal hypoautofluorescence corresponding with complete retinal pigment epithelium and outer retinal atrophy on OCT (Figureand insert). Automated 10-2 visual field testing revealed dense paracentral ring scotomata bilaterally.

options.A: Confirm hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity and recommend observation when not receiving therapy
options.C: Intravitreal injection of a complement inhibitor

distractors: Confirm hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity and recommend observation when not receiving therapy
Intravitreal injection of a complement inhibitor
explanation: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes This patient’s presentation was atypical for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity. Her pattern of perifoveal atrophy was more consistent with inherited mitochondrial disease, and ocular findings were discussed with neurology, medical genetics, and rheumatology teams in the context of progressive neurologic symptoms, which prompted genetic evaluation. Genetic testing revealed a pathogenicMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variation (heteroplasmy 23%), the most common variation causing mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and strokelike episodes (MELAS). MELAS, while relatively rare in the general population, is one of the more common mitochondrial myopathies, with a population-dependent prevalence between 0.18 and 236 per 100 000 individuals.1Similar to other mitochondrial diseases, MELAS is either maternally inherited or may arise from de novo mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variations, most commonly A to G transition at mtDNA position 3243.2,3Age at onset is variable but usually manifests before age 40 years with any combination of seizures, strokelike episodes, progressive cognitive deterioration, myopathy, and variable involvement of other organs.1,4,5Disease severity is impacted by heteroplasmy, the proportion of pathogenic mtDNA, and potentially by coexisting nuclear DNA sequence variations.6Potential associations include diabetes, sensorineural hearing loss, and cardiac disorders. The most common clinical presentation of retinopathy associated withMT-TL1m.3243A>G sequence variations is circumferential perifoveal atrophy, initially discontinuous, as in this patient, which may coalesce over time.4Fundus autofluorescence imaging typically demonstrates hypoautofluorescence in areas of advanced chorioretinal atrophy with surrounding speckled hyperautofluorescence. Other possible ocular manifestations include ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, cataract, and optic nerve atrophy.7Visual acuity is variable but often good at presentation.4 Diagnosis of MELAS may be confirmed with genetic testing in the context of relevant clinical findings (including encephalopathy and strokelike episodes), laboratory clues (including elevated lactate levels in serum and cerebrospinal fluid [CSF]), and muscle biopsy evaluating for ragged red fibers. Comprehensive systemic evaluation is imperative for identification and management of associated conditions. Management of MELAS is mainly supportive and also critically involves avoiding medications that can cause mitochondrial toxicity (eg, valproic acid) or lactic acidosis (eg, metformin).1Multiple studies have supported a role for arginine supplementation in the management and prevention of strokelike episodes,8as well as for other vitamins and supplements including coenzyme Q10, creatine, and carnitine as part of a “mitochondrial cocktail” for patients with mitochondrial cytopathies.9 Option A is incorrect. While discontinuing hydroxychloroquine may be reasonable in the context of this patient’s maculopathy,10further evaluation is warranted to make the appropriate diagnosis and to ensure appropriate monitoring, identification of associated systemic manifestations, genetic counseling, and potential evaluation of family members. Options B and C are incorrect. While there is outer retinal and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy on OCT, the patient is relatively young and lacks other findings consistent with age-related macular degeneration. The patient’s systemic manifestations of MELAS were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. Her evaluation revealed elevated lactic acid in the serum and CSF. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss for her age, with disproportionate cerebellum involvement and scattered chronic lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia and left thalamus. She was prescribed arginine, carnitine, and coenzyme Q10, as well as vitamins A, D, E, K, and a vitamin B complex. She continued insulin treatment for her diabetes, lactulose, rifaximin, and sodium benzoate for cirrhosis-associated encephalopathy, as well as antiepileptic medication.

caption: A, Acutely inflamed, denuded laryngeal squamous mucosa with submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation (original magnification ×100). B, Biopsy demonstrating oval yeast forms consistent withHistoplasma capsulatum(arrowheads) measuring 2 to 4 μm in diameter with narrow-based budding (original magnification ×400).
scenario: A 61-year-old man presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, and persistent globus sensation. He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, cough, or hemoptysis. He had a history of coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, peripheral vascular disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and ulcerative colitis. He reported no immunosuppressive therapy. He quit smoking 8 months prior after a 35–pack-year history and consumed alcohol infrequently. He denied recent travel, exposure to tuberculosis, or prior radiation to the head and neck. On physical examination, there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes or oropharyngeal abnormalities. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a fibrinous, ulcerative lesion on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis with surrounding edema and preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility. Given concern for cancer, the patient underwent direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Examination under anesthesia confirmed irregular mucosa with fibrinous exudate localized to the epiglottis. Histopathology results revealed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Figure, A). Grocott methenamine silver stain highlighted narrow-based budding yeast (Figure, B).
explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

caption: A, Sagittal T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging shows multiple hypointense lesions in the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae. B, Sagittal computed tomography image (soft tissue window) demonstrates mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction.
scenario: A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

options.A: Bone metastases from submandibular gland cancer

distractors: Bone metastases from submandibular gland cancer
explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

caption: A, Computed tomography showing a soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland with ill-defined margins. B, Low-powered stain of a multinodular lesion containing multiple blood-filled spaces, surrounded by dense inflammatory cell infiltration and encased within a thick fibrous capsule (original magnification ×20).
scenario: A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.
explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

caption: A, Clinical photograph demonstrating a lesion of the right mandibular angle. B, Coronal view of maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) showing a multiloculated lesion at the right mandibular angle. The lesion is expansile in nature and located inferior to inferior alveolar nerve. It demonstrates cortical invasion involving both the buccal and lingual aspects.
scenario: A healthy 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of a painful right mandibular lesion (Figure 1A). The patient reported progressive persistent pain and enlargement of the lesion since it was first noticed. She denied any facial trauma history and had no sensory deficits in the inferior alveolar nerve distribution or signs of infection such as purulent discharge, foul taste, warmth, or erythema of the overlying skin. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.
explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

caption: A, Intraoral photograph showing strawberrylike appearance of the gingivae. B, Low-powered hematoxylin-eosin stain of gingival mucosa with chronic inflammatory infiltrates and microabscesses (original magnification ×40).
scenario: A 69-year-old woman was referred to the to the oral and maxillofacial surgery department due to widespread gingival swelling, which had been progressively worsening over the preceding 3 months and was unresponsive to antibiotic treatment (amoxicillin and lincomycin). She experienced low-grade fever lasting for about 1 month, unresponsive to various antibiotics; general malaise; reduction of appetite; weight loss; and recurrent episodes of nasal bleeding. Moderate hypertension, well-controlled pharmacologically with ramipril and hydrochlorothiazide, was noted. On clinical examination, nontender gingival swelling was noted (Figure 1A), along with laterocervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. In particular, the upper anterior gingiva appeared markedly enlarged, erythematous, friable, and with a granular surface. Gingival biopsy showed areas of chronic inflammation, microabscess foci, and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the covering epithelium (Figure 1B), with findings regarded as nonspecific. Blood tests revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia, elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and fibrinogen), and hypergammaglobulinemia. Chest radiography performed during the hospital stay described a 1-cm nodule in the apical region of the right lung and another nodular image in the midfield of the left lung, and the subsequent contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography confirmed the presence of multiple solid nodular formations in both lungs. However, the fine-needle aspiration biopsy of these lesions was nondiagnostic due to insufficient material (essentially blood). A bone marrow biopsy described a partially fibrotic sample with a plasma cell population CD138+but was overall inconclusive. Due to her deteriorating conditions, the patient was given corticosteroidsex adiuvantibus(prednisone, 50 mg, once daily) with a rapid improvement of symptoms.
explanation: A pathology review of the gingival biopsy at a multidisciplinary team meeting described areas of necrotizing vasculitis and regions containing multinucleated giant cells (Figure 2). Based on the clinical, serological, and histopathological findings, a definitive diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly Wegener granulomatosis) was established. Subsequent lung biopsy confirmed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with vasculitis. Laboratory findings of positive anti–proteinase 3 (PR3) antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) corroborated this diagnosis. There are 3 forms of ANCA-associated vasculitides: these include GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic GPA. While all are multisystem diseases marked by inflammation of small blood vessels, GPA is specifically characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation that affects the ears, nose, and both the upper and lower respiratory tracts, along with necrotizing vasculitis that primarily involves small- to medium-sized vessels.1According to the most recent American College of Rheumatology/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification, this patient met the criteria for GPA, being positive for nasal involvement (bloody discharge), lung nodules, giant cells at biopsy, and anti-PR3 antibodies. While the distinct erythematous overripened strawberry appearance of the gingivae—often referred to as strawberry gums or strawberrylike gingivitis—is considered nearly pathognomonic,2oral cavity signs are not included in the most recent classification system. This likely reflects the low prevalence and, hence, scarce sensitivity of this manifestation. Oral lesions, including nonspecific ulcerations, have been reported in 10% to 60% of patients and may be the presenting sign of GPA in around 5% of cases.3In particular, strawberrylike gingivitis is the most common oral manifestation of GPA4and may be the initial disease manifestation in 2% of cases.5However, it is generally accepted that most oral manifestations appear during an advanced stage of the disease and are rarely an early indicator. The histopathological assessment of oral lesions in GPA is usually regarded as difficult, as the hallmark features of necrotizing granulomas and marked leukocytoclastic vasculitis are frequently absent. Instead, findings such as pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, multinucleated giant cells, and gingival microabscesses are more frequently encountered.6As a result, investigators often focus on a constellation of individual, typically nonspecific features, which, when present together, can suggest the diagnosis. Drug-induced gingival overgrowth is a common adverse effect of certain medications, particularly anticonvulsants (eg, phenytoin), calcium channel blockers (eg, nifedipine), and immunosuppressants (eg, cyclosporine).7It manifests as painless, firm gingival enlargement, often involving the anterior gingiva. To our knowledge, there are no reports to date of gingival overgrowth induced by ramipril. Furthermore, the presence of associated systemic symptoms (like fever, weight loss, and nasal bleeding) and histological findings of vasculitis ruled it out in this case. Sarcoidosis is a fairly common (10 to 20 cases per 100 000) multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown cause, marked by the formation of noncaseating granulomas in affected organs. It most commonly involves the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, and eyes but can occasionally affect the oral cavity. Notably, strawberry gums in sarcoidosis have been reported.8Diagnosis relies on clinical-radiologic findings and biopsy showing granulomas without necrosis, and it typically does not involve necrotizing vasculitis or upper airway bleeding like in GPA. Hematological malignant tumors including leukemia, lymphomas (particularly non-Hodgkin lymphoma), and multiple myeloma can cause gingival enlargement due to neoplastic infiltration, along with systemic symptoms like anemia, fever, and lymphadenopathy.9In acute leukemias, particularly acute myeloid leukemia and acute monocytic leukemia, gingival hypertrophy and swelling are common due to leukemic infiltration of the gingival tissues. While the suspicion of monoclonal gammopathy, such as multiple myeloma, may warrant further investigation, also in view of the possible oral manifestations,10the lack of abnormal white blood cell infiltration in the biopsy and in the bone marrow and the presence of granulomatous vasculitis made a hematologic malignant tumor less likely.

caption: Computed tomography scan of the anterior calvarium.
scenario: A 48-year old woman presented with a 4-week history of episodic headaches and light sensitivity. She reported falling on her head, which marked the onset of her headaches. Within 3 weeks, she noticed a painful, pulsating mass on the right side of her forehead, which she initially attributed to the fall. She also had a history of hypertension, which worsened the symptoms of headaches and the swelling of the mass. She denied experiencing fever, chills, night sweats, or any changes in her vision. The patient’s medical history was significant for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and thyroid nodules that were previously biopsied as benign. At that point, her medication history included 4 months of semaglutide, along with metformin and losartan. She formerly smoked. The physical examination and imaging revealed a 2.5-cm mass/swelling on the right frontal calvarium (Figure 1). Imaging results were significant for thyromegaly, but no other sites of metastatic disease were observed in the chest, abdomen, or pelvis. The mass was biopsied, revealing a 1.6-cm right anterior calvarial lesion, which prompted a neurosurgery referral for further evaluation. She underwent resection of the right frontal calvarial mass and cranioplasty reconstruction.
explanation: C. Metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma The pathology report of the anterior calvarial lesion biopsy specimen revealed a follicle-forming tumor of thyroid origin that was consistent with metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma, and the patient was subsequently referred for further thyroid evaluation. Although previous nodule biopsy specimens revealed benign cysts, recent computed tomography of the neck revealed partially calcified and heterogeneously enhancing nodules. Total thyroidectomy was completed, revealing a 5.6-cm thyroid tumor. Pathology results showed poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTC) arising from a background of follicular thyroid carcinoma and T3aN0M1 staging. PDTC is in the category of high-grade follicular, cell-derived nonanaplastic thyroid carcinoma, with a definition of neoplasm of thyroid follicular cells with high-grade features with mitotic count and tumor necrosis without anaplastic histology. In this case, resection specimen showed a solid growth pattern of follicular cells with multifocal capsular invasion and focal lymphatic invasion. Tumor nests demonstrated solid/trabecular architecture with minimal to no colloid (Figure 2A). There was no papillary architecture or papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclear feature identified in this case. Tumor cells were small to medium size, with round nuclei, indistinct nucleoli, and a lack of anaplasia. Occasional nuclei show convoluted and irregular contours. Large zonal necrosis and increased mitosis (10 per 2 mm2) were identified (Figure 2B). Per Turin and World Health Organization criteria, this lesion is categorized as poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma.1 In general, PDTC has more aggressive behavior, and prognosis is between well-differentiated follicular carcinoma (such as papillary thyroid carcinoma or follicular carcinoma) and anaplastic carcinoma.2PDTC shows a higher T and N stage and 5-year survival rate is between 50% to 70%. Specific molecular alterations unique for PDTC are not identified, and they generally harborBRAF V600EorRAS,NRAS, andTERTvariants. A 2023 study showed somatic variants of ABCA12,CLIP1, andATP13A3were significantly associated with a vascular invasion phenotype.3 More than 40 000 individuals receive a diagnosis of thyroid cancer each year in the US.4The second most prevalent type of thyroid cancer is follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC), which arises from the follicular cells responsible for producing iodine-containing thyroid hormones.5Distant metastases occur in approximately 10% to 15% of FTC cases, with the bones and lungs being the most common sites.6Secondary skull metastases originating from FTC are rare, comprising only 2% to 5% of all skeletal metastases from the thyroid.7These cases are more common in female patients, with headaches being the most frequently reported symptom.7 In rare cases, patients with metastatic FTC can present with progressively enlarging frontal skull masses. The masses are firm, pulsatile, and fixed to the skull, with some cases exhibiting mobility.8In many instances, patients remain asymptomatic apart from the noticeable swelling, leading to delayed diagnosis.8However, patients who present with concurrent neck masses may experience compressive symptoms, such as difficulty swallowing or breathing.9Headaches are commonly reported, particularly in cases of hypertension that exacerbates the episodic headaches as described in this article. Patients may also develop neurological symptoms, such as seizures and light sensitivity.9,10 In their systematic review of 20 patients with secondary skull analysis from FTC, Scalia et al7highlighted that FTC skull metastases predominantly affect women (mean age, 65.6 years). Some patients presented with isolated skull masses (most commonly in the anterior calvarium), while others had concurrent thyroid lesions. In cases in which FTC metastases progress, symptoms such as headaches became more prominent (70% of reported cases).7Despite the differences in presentation, the overall clinical pattern remains consistent: painless, slow-growing skull masses that may be accompanied with an enlarged thyroid gland. These findings emphasize the importance of timely imaging studies, referrals, and biopsies in diagnosing FTC metastases to confirm thyroid origin and implement proper treatment to ensure good patient outcomes.

scenario: A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Right lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forTTF-1, napsin A, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative forPAX8and thyroglobulin.
