options.B: Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant
options.D: Metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma with atypical pulmonary spread

answer: Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant
distractors: Metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma with atypical pulmonary spread
explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

caption: Preoperative photograph of midline tongue defect.
scenario: A male infant aged 2 weeks presented to an otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a tongue lesion. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via caesarean delivery that was complicated by preeclampsia. Prenatal ultrasonography and subsequent magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated concern for a tongue cyst. At birth, a small midline tongue defect was noted, for which the patient was referred to an ear, nose, and throat clinic. At the time of the initial evaluation, he was feeding well and gaining weight appropriately. He was found to have a shallow, midline tongue depression with no discrete masses or lesions. Recommendations were for a watchful waiting approach to allow for granulation of the defect. The patient presented for follow-up approximately 2 years later, with his parents reporting concerns for persistence of the lesion. He was also having issues with food trapping in the area of the defect. He was found to have an approximately 1-cm anterior midline tongue indentation (Figure 1), and surgical excision was recommended. Following surgical excision, histopathologic examination of the excised tract demonstrated squamous and respiratory mucosa with regional striated muscle bundles, smooth muscle, adipose tissue, and minor salivary glands.
explanation: The foregut gives rise to the pharynx, lower respiratory tract, and upper gastrointestinal tract, including the esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and hepatobiliary system. Foregut duplication cysts, also known as enteric duplication cysts (EDCs), result from abnormal embryologic development (Figure 2). Their precise etiology is not well understood, and multiple theories have been proposed to explain their origin. To our knowledge, there is no single unifying explanation for the variety of EDCs that can occur throughout the body. The aberrant budding theory is commonly used to explain esophageal and bronchogenic cysts. According to this theory, outpouchings develop from the primitive gut tube and become isolated from the main tract. These outpouchings are lined with secretory epithelium, allowing fluid accumulation and cyst formation. Another proposed mechanism involves errors during the recanalization of the primitive gut tube. In this scenario, failure of recanalization results in the formation of isolated tubular structures that retain fluid and persist during development. The split notochord theory is the most widely accepted embryologic explanation for enteric cysts in general. It suggests that an abnormal connection forms between the notochord and the primitive gut tube that results in persistent adhesions and anomalous development. This theory is useful in explaining neurenteric cysts; however, it does not readily explain the presence of cysts within the oral cavity.1-3 EDCs, or enterocystomas, can theoretically occur anywhere along the gastrointestinal tract. Most frequently, they are found in the thorax or abdomen, particularly near the esophagus or small bowel.4In contrast, cysts of the head and neck region are exceedingly rare, accounting for fewer than 1% of all EDCs. Among these rare head and neck occurrences, the oral cavity is the most common location.4When in the oral cavity, they can also be known as lingual choristomas.5 Most cysts (approximately 80%) present before age 2 years. Prenatal ultrasonography may detect enteric duplications as early as 16 weeks of gestational age but is only possible in 20% to 30% of cases.2,5Postnatally, magnetic resonance imaging is the imaging modality of choice. It provides soft tissue contrast and can delineate the extent of the cyst, its relationship to adjacent structures, and the presence of any associated anomalies. However, EDCs cannot be reliably distinguished from dermoid cysts or other cystic lesions based on imaging alone. In one study that evaluated 6 pediatric patients with oral cavity EDCs, all were misdiagnosed before surgical excision.3,5 Definitive diagnosis requires histopathologic confirmation. Classically, 3 criteria must be met: (1) the cyst must be surrounded by a smooth muscle layer; (2) it must be lined with gastrointestinal, gastric, or respiratory epithelium; and (3) it must be attached to a structure derived from the foregut.2Therefore, a diagnosis can only be made after surgical excision or biopsy, when tissue can be evaluated microscopically. Clinically, oral EDCs may be asymptomatic or may present with airway compromise, respiratory distress, or feeding difficulties, particularly in neonates and infants. In emergent situations, needle decompression can provide temporary relief, but complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Even when a cyst has ruptured, excision is still recommended. Retention of the cyst may result in progressive enlargement, mass effect, or recurrent infection. While cyst recurrence is rare, it is possible if the secretory epithelium is not completely removed.3 In summary, oral foregut duplication cysts are rare congenital anomalies that present diagnostic and management challenges. Awareness of their embryologic basis, clinical presentation, and imaging limitations is essential for prompt diagnosis and appropriate surgical treatment. Early recognition and excision lead to excellent outcomes and reduce the risk of complications or recurrence. The patient’s postoperative course was uncomplicated. At follow-up, he had resumed a regular diet and was no longer having issues with food trapping.

caption: A, Axial computed tomography (CT) in bone window showing spiculated periosteal reaction (arrowhead) within the right frontal bone with associated soft tissue component. B, Corresponding axial T2-weighted magnetic resonance image (MRI) showing a predominantly T2 hypointense soft tissue mass in the right orbitofrontal region.
scenario: A 3-month-old male infant presented with a painless, gradually enlarging swelling in their right orbital and temporal region over 2 months. Examination revealed a firm, nontender, 5 × 4-cm mass with proptosis. The overlying skin exhibited a slight bluish discoloration. Computed tomography (CT) showed a large lytic lesion with a soft tissue component and spiculated, aggressive type of periosteal reaction with mild hyperostosis of the underlying bone. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a precontrast T1 hyperintense lesion with few hypointense areas, T2 hypointense spiculations and intense postcontrast enhancement and mild diffusion restriction (Figure 1). Chest and abdominal screening using low-dose CT showed no distant disease. The tumor was excised with clear margins, and histopathology showed a biphasic pattern of small neuroblastlike cells and larger melanin-containing epithelial cells. No evidence of locoregional or distant recurrence was observed after 1 year of follow-up.
explanation: C. Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy (MNTI) is a rare, typically benign neoplasm almost exclusively affecting infants younger than 1 year, with a median age at diagnosis being 5 months. Historically termedmelanotic progonoma, this entity has been described in fewer than 500 cases in the literature.1,2More than 90% of cases involve the head and neck, most commonly the maxilla (60%-80%). Other affected sites include the skull, mandible, and less frequently, intracranial and extracraniofacial locations such as the epididymis, ovaries, and bones of the extremities.1-3Clinically, MNTI presents as a rapidly enlarging, firm, nontender mass, often pigmented due to melanin, though nonpigmented forms occur.2,4,5Presentation varies by site; maxillary tumors may interfere with feeding or displace teeth, while intracranial lesions can cause neurologic symptoms or raised intracranial pressure.3,6Mandibular lesions may cause pathologic fracture.1 CT typically shows a lytic, expansile lesion with enhancing soft tissue and, less commonly, a sunburst periosteal reaction, which is more frequent in calvarial than maxillary MNTIs.3,4,7MRI adds detail on soft tissue and melanin-related T1 signal changes (Figure 2). Diffusion restriction is usually present due to the high tumor cellularity.4T1 hyperintensity is quite specific for MNTI but lacks sensitivity, as not all cases show this feature.7Key differential includes neuroblastoma—another neuroectodermal tumor—which may show heterogeneous enhancement with calcifications and can metastasize to the orbit. Abdominal imaging (CT or ultrasonography) can help identify the primary site. Furthermore, although both entities may be associated with elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid levels, only neuroblastoma typically demonstrates uptake on a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan.8Other differentials include Ewing sarcoma, characterized by permeative lysis and aggressive periosteal reaction, but a disease of older children; while Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically presents as a punched-out lytic lesion with an associated soft tissue component in untreated cases and often lacks a periosteal reaction.9Histologically, MNTI shows a biphasic pattern (hallmark of the tumor) with large, melanin-rich epithelioid cells at the periphery and small, primitive neurogenic cells centrally, arranged in nests, cords, or pseudoalveolar structures within fibrocollagenous stroma.2,6Atypia, necrosis, and mitotic activity are generally absent.3On immunohistochemistry, large cells are positive for pan-cytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, vimentin, and HMB-45; small cells stain, with neuron specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. S100 is usually negative5,10Although definitive diagnosis requires biopsy,10imaging features combined with awareness of the typical age group can strongly suggest the diagnosis. Surgical excision with clear margins is the mainstay of treatment.1Complete resection may be limited by proximity to vital structures, especially in infants.2While less aggressive surgery may suffice in select cases, recurrence risk supports efforts at total removal. Adjuvant therapy is reserved for incomplete resection or aggressive disease; chemotherapy may be effective but lacks definitive outcome data.1,7Despite its benign nature, MNTI has a significant recurrence rate (10%-45%), usually within 1 to 2 years postsurgery.2Risk factors include early age, large tumor size, incomplete excision, and nonmaxillary sites. Malignant transformation and metastasis are rare but reported.2 Close follow-up is essential due to recurrence risk.5Surveillance typically includes clinical exams and MRI at regular intervals for early detection.2,6Long-term monitoring is advised to address late recurrence or treatment-related complications.5

scenario: A woman in her early 50s presented with a neck mass, incidentally discovered during evaluation of recurrent headaches. She reported mild solid food dysphagia but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed fullness in the location of the left thyroid lobe. Flexible laryngoscopy showed normal vocal fold movement and laboratory findings were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.4-cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left thyroid lobe, with suggestion of a feeding vessel (Figure 1). An ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration for the presumed thyroid nodule was performed, but definitive characterization was not possible with the limited material obtained. Therefore, a 20-gauge core biopsy was attempted but was aborted due to patient discomfort. Because of the unclear diagnosis, she was scheduled for a left thyroid lobectomy with excision of the mass. Postoperatively, she experienced resolution of her dysphagia and vocal fold function was normal.
explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

caption: A, Bilateral supraclavicular masses with an ulcerative necrotic midline neck lesion. The red pigment from the tattoo was partially replaced by pale areas of cross-scarring (arrowhead). B, Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated ill-defined heterogeneous iso-/hypointense signal on coronal T1-weighted imaging with predominantly peripheral enhancement and adjacent vascular compression.
scenario: A 20-year-old man presented with bilateral neck masses that gradually increased in size for over 5 months following a red cross tattoo on his anterior neck. Three months after the tattoo, the red ink spontaneously faded and was replaced by atrophic scars and necrotic ulcers with light bloody exudation. Initial management with antibiotics and topical corticosteroids yielded no improvement. Physical examination revealed firm, ill-defined cervical and submental lymphadenopathy bilaterally, alongside a midline anterior neck mass demonstrating cutaneous invasion, ulceration, and crusting (Figure 1A). No systemic symptom was observed. Laboratory tests including complete blood cell count, tuberculosis T-cell gamma interferon assay, serum IgG4, and complete immune testing results were within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated ill-defined infiltrative masses measuring 3.8 × 2.9 cm and 3.4 × 4.2 cm on both sides of the neck and 4.9 × 3.5 cm in the suprasternal fossa. The lesions showed heterogeneous iso-/hyperintense signal on T1-weighted imaging and hyper-/hypointense signal on T2-weighted imaging, with contrast-enhanced lesions showing predominantly peripheral enhancement. The internal jugular vein in the lower part of the neck was invisible, leaving vague hyperintense signal embedded in the mass (Figure 1B). Enhanced computed tomography implied bilateral internal jugular vein thrombosis as well. Repeated fine-needle aspiration yielded necrotic debris, eosinophilic and lymphocyte-dominated inflammation, and fibrosis, which were insufficient for a definitive diagnosis. Given concern regarding the radiographic features and clinical progression, surgical excision with bilateral internal jugular vein ligation and free rectus femoris flap reconstruction was performed.

options.B: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis

distractors: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis
explanation: C. Tattoo-associated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis Histopathological examination showed reactive lymphoid hyperplasia with extensive necrosis, chronic inflammatory cell infiltration (predominantly lymphocytes and plasma cells), and noncaseating granuloma formation. The histological features of inflammatory emboli in the internal jugular vein are similar with that of cervical lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed SMA-positive myofibroblastoma cells, but pan-cytokeratin, IgG4, S-100, SOX10, and CD34 were negative. Acid-fast bacilli staining was negative, and mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR failed to detect mycobacterial DNA. Epstein-Barr virus–encoded RNA staining was negative. These findings collectively supported a diagnosis of necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis. Tattooing has emerged as a modern cultural phenomenon associated with personal expression. However, its potential adverse effects, ranging from infections to neoplastic complications, demand heightened clinical awareness. Emerging evidence suggests a possible association between tattoos and malignant neoplasms such as lymphoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, with a higher incidence observed in tattooed populations.1 Granulomatous reactions to tattoo pigments, typically classified as delayed hypersensitivity responses, manifest histopathologically as granuloma annulare or perforating granulomas confined to tattooed regions.2Clinically, these present as pruritic, erythematous nodules or lichenoid changes, rarely extending into deeper tissues.3Heavy metals (eg, mercury, cadmium) and organic dyes (notably red pigments) in tattoo pigments are implicated in triggering delayed-type hypersensitivity or foreign-body granulomas. While pigment deposition within lesions is a consistent histopathological hallmark, necrosis remains uncommon, with only one other reported case, to our knowledge.4 Lymphatic migration of tattoo pigments may result in lymphadenopathy characterized by painless enlargement and intranodal pigment accumulation, often mimicking metastasis. Imaging modalities such as positron emission tomography–computed tomography frequently fail to differentiate pigment-laden nodes from malignant metastasis, underscoring the necessity of meticulous tattoo history documentation and histopathologic confirmation.5Furthermore, hematogenous dissemination of pigments to distant organs (eg, liver) has been reported, potentially leading to misdiagnosis as metastatic melanoma, particularly in high-risk cohorts.6 Unlike conventional granulomatous reactions, this patient exhibited aggressive local invasion, deep cervical lymphadenopathy, and jugular inflammatory thrombus in the absence of systemic symptoms or infectious etiologies. Thrombus formation in benign inflammatory contexts is previously reported only in association with invasive infections or malignant neoplasms. We propose 3 potential mechanisms: (1) venous wall erosion secondary to granulomatous lymphadenitis, (2) a hypercoagulable state induced by chronic inflammation and cytokine dysregulation (eg, IL-6-mediated fibrinogen production), and (3) vascular stasis due to mass compression by enlarged lymph nodes. This case distinguishes from prior reports of necrotizing granulomas confined to the tattooed skin with minimal deep infiltration. Lymph node involvement preceded local skin reactions, which favored the diagnosis. Notably, red tattoo pigment was absent in resected lesions despite histopathological and clinical correlation supporting the diagnosis. This report expands the spectrum of tattoo-associated pathology. Clinicians should remain highly suspicious of tattoo-related etiologies in patients presenting with necrotic neck masses, even in the absence of visible pigment. Vascular invasion necessitates urgent evaluation, as thrombosis may require immediate intervention. While topical corticosteroid therapy proves ineffective, complete surgical excision remains the cornerstone of both diagnosis and management. The patient finally recovered under the comprehensive treatment mode of surgical operation, short-term systemic hormone therapy, and infection prevention.

caption: Clinical image of the ulcer in the left buccal mucosa. The ulcer was present for 1 month, covered by a grayish-yellow fibrinopurulent membrane, and was painful.
scenario: A healthy 69-year-old man presented with a painful, progressively enlarging ulcer located on the left buccal mucosa, persisting for more than 1 month. No significant medical history and no other associated symptoms or contributory factors were identified. On clinical examination, a large ulcer in the buccal mucosa adjacent was observed to the third molar region. The ulcer was 3 × 2 cm, grayish-yellow and shallow in nature, had smooth, well-demarcated borders covered by a fibrinopurulent membrane, and was painful (Figure 1). The specimen was submitted for pathology with a provisional diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. Although the patient had no underlying medical conditions, he reported using tirzepatide for weight loss over the past 6 months and an occupation involving long-term exposure to nitrous oxide. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography of the skull base to mid-thigh was done after the pathology report to rule out any evidence of tumor. Large focus of intensive fludeoxyglucose-18 uptake was noted in the left oral cavity with slight evidence of left maxillary bone erosion. No other mass lesions or invasive growth were noted elsewhere.
explanation: B. Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer The given condition was diagnosed as Epstein-Barr virus–associated mucocutaneous ulcer (EBVMCU). The ulcer was a localized, shallow, well-defined mass covered with a fibrinopurulent membrane. In contrast, oral squamous cell carcinoma typically presents with nonhomogeneous, nodulo-proliferative, warty ulcers. Ulcers caused by deep fungal infections often appear irregular and necrotic and may be deeper or multifocal. Oral lymphomas, often associated with EBV, may present with ulceration but are generally accompanied by other symptoms, such as swelling and lymphadenopathy, and typically do not resolve quickly. EBVMCU was first described by Dojcinov et al1as a lymphoproliferative disorder presenting as a sharply defined cutaneous or mucosal ulcer, often associated with immunosuppression (autoimmune medication, posttransplant therapy, age-related immunosenescence, HIV infection).2To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of EBVMCU associated with immunosuppression possibly related to tirzepatide use. Histological analysis revealed ulcerated epithelium with extensive necrosis and fibrinopurulent exudate in the underlying connective tissue. Clusters of large atypical lymphoid cells with Hodgkinlike features were observed. Patchy fibrino-hemorrhagic necrosis and focal angioinvasion were present. A diffuse polymorphous infiltrate of intermediate-sized immunoblasts, epithelioid histiocytes, and large pleomorphic Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg (HRS)–like cells were noted. These cells showed strong positivity for EBER in situ hybridization, PAX5, CD3, CD20, and CD30 (Figure 2). The histological differential diagnoses include EBV-positive lymphoproliferative disorders, such as classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) and aggressive EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). EBVMCU can be distinguished by its polymorphous infiltrate, CD45-positive HRS-like cells, and lack of systemic involvement. EBVMCU is EBER positive, but unlike DLBCL, this positivity is generally restricted to B cells within the ulcer. Additionally, CD45 positivity in HRS-like cells helps differentiate EBVMCU from cHL.3,4The etiology of EBVMCU is not fully understood, but immunosuppression and advanced age are the primary risk factors. Dojcinov et al1reported 9 cases related to immunosuppressive medication (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine A) and 17 cases related to age-related immunosenescence. Cases in immunocompetent individuals have also been described. One hypothesis suggests that mucosal trauma may lead to persistent stimulation and activation of B-lymphocytes, resulting in transformation due to EBV persistence. Impaired EBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell response may allow for unchecked B-cell and natural killer/T-cell proliferation.2 Tirzepatide, used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes, is associated with gastrointestinal tract adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, and reduced appetite. In this case, such effects may have contributed to transient immunosuppression, leading to EBVMCU.5The patient also reported occupational nitrous oxide exposure. Studies have shown that long-term nitrous oxide inhalation showed significantly higher levels of interferon-γ and IL-4 concentrations. Although not validated clinically, long-term nitrous oxide inhalation has been shown to alter immune function markers, potentially contributing to subclinical immunosuppression.6 Following discontinuation of tirzepatide, the ulcer showed progressive healing within 1 month. Oncology consultation led to supportive treatment for EBVMCU, and there has been no evidence of disease recurrence at 6-month follow-up. Early diagnosis of EBVMCU is crucial to distinguish it from aggressive lymphoproliferative malignant neoplasms and to avoid unnecessary treatments. EBVMCU generally follows an indolent course and may resolve spontaneously or with minimal intervention.7In contrast, cHL, oral lymphomas, and DLBCL require intensive therapy. A thorough clinical history—including immunosuppressive medications or immune-modulating agents, like tirzepatide—plays a key role in diagnosis. While symptom resolution followed drug cessation in this case, further research is needed to explore a definitive causal relationship.

caption: A, Axial T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrates a well-defined, encapsulated lesion in the root of the tongue, appearing isointense relative to adjacent skeletal muscle. B, Axial T2-weighted MRI shows the same lesion with heterogeneous high signal intensity and multiple internal ringlike structures, suggesting cystic or myxoid degeneration.
scenario: A 32-year-old female patient presented to our clinic with a 4-month history of progressive tongue roughness and a sensation of fullness. She denied associated symptoms, including otalgia, dysphonia, dysphagia, odynophagia, dyspnea, or weight loss. On oral examination, tongue protrusion revealed leftward deviation with restricted mobility, particularly toward the contralateral side. There was a subtle bulge at the posterior floor of the mouth, but no visible mucosal lesions. Bimanual palpation of the tongue revealed a deep, firm, nontender mass localized to the central posterior tongue. The overlying mucosa was smooth and intact, with no signs of ulceration or erythema. No cervical lymphadenopathy was detected. Nasopharyngolaryngoscopy demonstrated normal vocal cord mobility; however, the oropharynx was significantly narrowed due to the mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-defined, encapsulated lesion in the root of the tongue, measuring 63 × 40 × 45 mm. On axial postcontrast T1-weighted imaging, the lesion appeared isointense with mild heterogeneous enhancement (Figure 1A), while T2-weighted imaging demonstrated heterogeneous hyperintensity with internal ringlike structures (Figure 1B).
explanation: Schwannomas are rare tumors of the oral cavity, accounting for less than 1% of all head and neck neoplasms.1The tongue is one of the most common intraoral sites, typically involving the hypoglossal or lingual nerve. Tongue schwannomas represent a small fraction of benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors. They can occur at any age but are most frequently diagnosed in the third to fifth decades of life, with no significant sex predilection. These tumors are primarily slow growing and asymptomatic, often discovered incidentally or only once they grow large enough to cause mechanical obstruction or interfere with speech or swallowing. On examination, tongue schwannomas are usually submucosal and well-defined; however, assessment of texture, mobility, and fixation is important to differentiate them from more aggressive lesions.1-4 MRI plays a pivotal role in preoperative diagnosis and assessment; its superior soft tissue contrast allows for precise localization and detailed assessment of tumor size, location, and relationship to surrounding structures, which is essential for referral and surgical planning. Sagittal postcontrast T1-weighted MRI clearly delineated the craniocaudal extent and displacement of adjacent structures without evidence of invasion (Figure 2). On MRI, schwannomas typically appear as well-demarcated lesions that are hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images. They often exhibit the split-fat sign, which refers to a rim of surrounding fat visible on T1-weighted imaging, an indicator of a well-encapsulated, slowly growing lesion.1,4,5Gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows schwannomas as bright lesions with heterogeneous enhancement, due to their cellular heterogeneity, which reflects varying degrees of vascularity and tissue density.4,6MRI is crucial in differentiating schwannomas from malignant tumors, such as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Differentiation of tongue schwannomas from malignant or other benign submucosal lesions is important. SCC is the most common tumor of the tongue. SCCs are aggressive tumors that commonly arise in this mucosa and will exhibit deep invasion.7SCCs of a similar magnitude most often have an appearance that is painful (otalgia), ulcerative, and highly aggressive with lymphatic spread. Common MRI findings suggest poorly defined, infiltrative borders and heterogeneous enhancement.4,7 Granular cell tumors are often mistaken for schwannomas, present as firm submucosal nodules, and show moderate enhancement on MRI but lack the T2 hyperintensity and fascicular architecture of schwannomas. Histopathology remains essential for differentiation.2,3,7 Salivary gland tumors arising from minor salivary glands are typically submucosal in location and may be benign or malignant. They appear well defined with smooth, pushing borders with cystic changes and moderate enhancement patterns on MRI.6,7Lipomas are benign fatty tumors that are soft to the touch, appear hyperintense on T1-weighted imaging, and lack gadolinium enhancement due to fat content, differentiating them from schwannomas.1,5,7 The clinical course of tongue schwannomas is typically indolent, with slow progression over months or years. This female patient experienced fullness and roughness for nearly 4 months before presentation. Schwannomas are encapsulated, allowing for successful enucleation with minimal risk of recurrence.1-4,8She underwent surgical excision at a tertiary center. Complete surgical excision remains the standard of care. Postoperative histopathological examination of the excised tumor, essential to rule out a malignant tumor, confirmed schwannoma. Schwannomas, particularly long-standing lesions, may demonstrate degenerative features, such as cystic change, nuclear atypia, and calcification termedancient change,which can mimic malignant tumors and require careful histologic interpretation2,3,9The patient recovered well postoperatively, with no evidence of recurrence or functional impairment. MRI remains the imaging modality of choice for preoperative planning and postoperative monitoring. Although schwannomas and malignant tumors may both exhibit restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging, schwannomas demonstrate higher mean apparent diffusion coefficient values due to their heterogeneous cellular and myxoid architecture.5,10Integration of diffusion-weighted imaging with conventional MRI features, such as well-defined encapsulation, enhances differentiation between these entities. This case report highlights the importance of thorough clinical and radiological evaluation, particularly MRI sequences, in the assessment of patients with submucosal tongue lesions. Tongue schwannomas, though rare, should be considered in the diagnosis and differentiated from malignant or other benign lesions. Adequate radiological assessment and histopathological confirmation are essential to ensure accurate diagnosis and optimal patient outcomes.

caption: Posteriorly based tracheal mass visualized on sagittal T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (A) and direct bronchoscopy (B).
scenario: A 17-year-old male adolescent with no significant medical history presented to his pediatrician with a 3-day history of sore throat and progressive shortness of breath. The patient began experiencing exertional dyspnea and “noisy” respirations 4 months ago. He denied fever, nasal congestion, or cough. Chest and lateral neck radiographs revealed a soft tissue density within the trachea. He was referred to the emergency department for further evaluation and treatment. The patient appeared well on presentation, with normal vital signs and laboratory values. He was breathing comfortably with room air without audible stridor or wheezing. Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated a tracheal mass. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck with contrast was obtained (Figure 1A). The patient was taken to the operating room for direct laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and biopsy (Figure 1B). Under suspension laryngoscopy, a cuffed endotracheal tube was carefully passed beyond the lesion, and the mass was partially debulked using cup forceps.
explanation: Pleomorphic adenoma (PA) is the most prevalent benign tumor of the salivary glands. Approximately 80% to 90% of PAs occur in the parotid gland. Most remaining cases are found in the submandibular or minor salivary glands, with the palate being the most common site for these tumors in the minor salivary glands.1A PA originating in the trachea is exceedingly rare, with fewer than 50 cases reported in the literature.2-4These lesions arise from heterotopic salivary gland tissue within the tracheal wall. Clinical presentation varies depending on the tumor’s location and degree of airway obstruction. Reported symptoms include cough, wheezing, stridor, and compressive symptoms such as dysphagia.3-6 The histology of PA includes a triphasic mixture of epithelial (ductal) cells, myoepithelial cells, and chondromyxoid stroma. Immunohistochemistry may support diagnosis7; pleomorphic adenoma gene 1 (PLAG1) staining is often positive and serves as a surrogate marker for underlyingPLAG1fusion (chromosome 8q12), the most prevalent genetic alteration found in PA.8In this case, a triphasic mixture was observed (Figure 2), and PLAG1 demonstrated nuclear positivity in each component, with strongest expression in cells surrounding ductal structures, consistent with the characteristic staining pattern of PA.8,9 Complete surgical excision is the standard of care for PAs.10Definitive treatment of airway PA would typically involve a segmental tracheal resection with end-to-end anastomosis.2,3Endoscopic resection or repeated debulking may be considered in selected cases, although the risk of recurrence and malignant transformation remains a concern. Given this patient’s young age, a segmental tracheal resection was performed without tracheostomy. Long-term surveillance, including endoscopic and radiologic evaluations, is recommended, although standardized follow-up protocols have not been established. Although PA is a familiar diagnosis in head and neck pathology, this case illustrates the importance of including PA in the differential diagnosis when evaluating airway lesions, as these common tumors may present in highly unusual locations.
